subsubtopic: CLOSING OF HAWKER SIDDELEY FORGE OPERATION-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise pursuant to Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. In view of the action presently under way by the management of Hawker Siddeley Canada Limited to dismantle their forge at Trenton, Nova Scotia, the largest such operation in Canada, in view of the great strategic and industrial importance of this unique facility to Canada, and in view of the possible efforts that this course of action will have on the work force of Hawker Siddeley's Trenton operations, as well as the interests of the industries which have grown to depend on the capacity of this forge for special projects, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Egmont (Mr. MacDonald):
That the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion and the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce forthwith instruct the management of Hawker Siddeley Canada Ltd. to immediately cease the dismantling of this unique forge and the machine shop used in connection therewith, until suitable alternatives have been discussed and arranged.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask a question of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources arising out of a story in this morning's Montreal Gazette that the president of Interprovincial Pipe Lines, Mr. Waldon, appears to be of the opinion that work on the extension of the pipeline to Montreal may not be started or will not be started until the spring of 1975, with the result that there will be another year's delay in the pipeline coming on stream. Is the government taking energetic steps to avoid the delay which the president of Interprovincial Pipe Lines apparently expects and perhaps even welcomes?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: OIL PIPELINE EXTENSION TO MONTREAL-STEPS TO AVOID DELAY IN COMMENCEMENT OF CONSTRUCTION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it strikes me that Mr. Wal-don's comments were related to the length of the regulatory proceedings that would precede construction and the possibility of telescoping the time frame of those proceedings without doing prejudice to the public interest required by the National Energy Board Act. subtopic: OIL PIPELINE EXTENSION TO MONTREAL-STEPS TO AVOID DELAY IN COMMENCEMENT OF CONSTRUCTION

REPLY TO DEMANDS BY SYNCRUDE CONSORTIUM
speechtext: The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources is, of course, aware of the fact that Syncrude made certain demands on the federal government. They first asked for a reply by November 16 and then decided to extend that a month to December 16, which is next Sunday. What demands has the Syncrude consortium made and has the federal government replied to any of those demands?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: REPLY TO DEMANDS BY SYNCRUDE CONSORTIUM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe my colleague, the Minister of Finance, has dealt with the response in relation to the taxation problem. I think a brief summary of that would be that the parties to the transaction have amended the nature of the transaction so that it would fit
Oral Questions
within the federal income tax law as it exists rather than requiring an amendment or some kind of special exemption. With regard to the question of pricing in particular, the companies had inquired as to the prospects of there being an assured price for the Syncrude product at a level which would enable the development to go ahead. We have indicated to them, in line with the comments made by the Prime Minister in his statement of last week, that a pricing policy would be envisaged which would enable higher cost resources to be brought on stream. One further element would be the risk of the project having to be run at less than optimum capacity because of shut-in requirements. We have agreed that the tar sands project, because of the necessity to have an optimum operation, would not be subject to the same risk of being shut in as would, for example, a conventional well.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Prime Minister. In view of the right hon. gentleman's advice to eastern Canada two days ago, "If you cannot afford foreign oil, don't buy it," I wonder if he could indicate briefly what plans the government has for this winter, perhaps in conjunction with provincial administrations, to provide some alternative source of fuel, or does he have any policy in this regard?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: OIL-MEASURES TO ASSIST EASTERN CANADIANS TO COPE WITH HIGH PRICES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. gentleman has misconstrued my remarks.

subtopic: OIL-MEASURES TO ASSIST EASTERN CANADIANS TO COPE WITH HIGH PRICES
speechtext: You said it. We heard it. It is that simple.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: OIL-MEASURES TO ASSIST EASTERN CANADIANS TO COPE WITH HIGH PRICES
speechtext:
The question seems to have been, what would we do to make sure that the price of offshore oil

December 14, 1973

would be lowered, or something along those lines. With regard to the consuming end, we have indicated various responses. I summed them up in my speech. I would refer the hon. member to it. I would also remind him that we suggested that in January we would be discussing with the provinces the measures or approaches we might take jointly to meet any further problems that might subsist.

subtopic: OIL-MEASURES TO ASSIST EASTERN CANADIANS TO COPE WITH HIGH PRICES
speechtext: I thank the Prime Minister for his very interesting answer. I do not want in any way to be unfair to him, but he did say a couple of days ago, as recorded at page 8669 of Hansard, that the federal government can in no way determine the price at which-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: OIL-MEASURES TO ASSIST EASTERN CANADIANS TO COPE WITH HIGH PRICES
speechtext: Order, please. I wonder whether we might not try to have questions rather than debate. Perhaps the hon. member could ask the question directly rather than referring to a prior statement. It might be easier for the Chair if that were done.

subtopic: OIL-MEASURES TO ASSIST EASTERN CANADIANS TO COPE WITH HIGH PRICES
speechtext: All right, Mr. Speaker. Perhaps the right hon. gentleman could indicate to us what specific measures he has for the short term. I indicated to him before that I wondered whether he was considering a short term subsidy or some other means to protect the people of the five eastern provinces of Canada from the very critical situation which is compounded by problems of transportation and supply from offshore sources. Surely he must have some specific measure so the people of eastern Canada will know how they are going to heat their homes this winter.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: OIL-MEASURES TO ASSIST EASTERN CANADIANS TO COPE WITH HIGH PRICES
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Speaker. In an earlier statement I indicated that the Minister of National Health and Welfare had communicated with the provinces, for instance, to ensure that our Canada Assistance Plan payments would be adequate to help those who are on welfare. I also indicated the escalation of various payments, family allowances and so on, which are now going toward offsetting the higher cost of living.

subtopic: OIL-MEASURES TO ASSIST EASTERN CANADIANS TO COPE WITH HIGH PRICES
speechtext: Give them a little welfare and hope they make it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: OIL-MEASURES TO ASSIST EASTERN CANADIANS TO COPE WITH HIGH PRICES
speechtext: If the hon. member is arguing that the federal government alone should bear the responsibility for these higher prices, I would just say that is not our view. Those provinces have for many years benefited from lower world prices compared with the people west of the Ottawa Valley line.

subtopic: OIL-MEASURES TO ASSIST EASTERN CANADIANS TO COPE WITH HIGH PRICES
speechtext: So let them freeze now.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: OIL-MEASURES TO ASSIST EASTERN CANADIANS TO COPE WITH HIGH PRICES
speechtext: It is not a question of letting them freeze. It is a question of who should pay the subsidy. I do not think the federal government should assume, as hon. members opposite are, that the taxpayers of all Canada should alone subsidize the people of certain provinces. I think the provincial governments themselves have some responsibility in this regard, particularly in view of the fact for years they have levied higher taxes on that cheaper oil in their provinces.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: OIL-MEASURES TO ASSIST EASTERN CANADIANS TO COPE WITH HIGH PRICES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question for the Prime Minister. Because of the fact that for a number of years there has been a balance in favour of Quebec and the eastern provinces in terms of the price of crude which never exceeded 50 cents a barrel, is it the Prime Minister's position that this justifies a national policy which involves the five eastern provinces paying perhaps an additional $3 a barrel? Is it the position of the Prime Minister that, because there has been a balance, sometimes as much as 50 cents a barrel, in favour of the Atlantic provinces and Quebec in terms of the price of crude, those provinces should be left to bear the cost of crude oil running as much as $3 or more a barrel more than the rest of Canada?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: OIL-MEASURES TO ASSIST EASTERN CANADIANS TO COPE WITH HIGH PRICES
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker. It is the government's position that the provincial governments have some responsibility in assisting the citizens of their provinces, that the federal taxpayer, that is to say, taxpayers from every part of Canada, should not be asked to subsidize a loan to the eastern consumers in this particular circumstance. The government intends bringing forth propositions to the federal-provincial conference-

subtopic: OIL-MEASURES TO ASSIST EASTERN CANADIANS TO COPE WITH HIGH PRICES
speechtext: What are they?

subtopic: OIL-MEASURES TO ASSIST EASTERN CANADIANS TO COPE WITH HIGH PRICES
speechtext: There are six very cold weeks ahead.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: OIL-MEASURES TO ASSIST EASTERN CANADIANS TO COPE WITH HIGH PRICES
speechtext: If members opposite would support us in a unilateral declaration policy, I would be glad to state it now, but they have often been urging us to consult with the provinces.

subtopic: OIL-MEASURES TO ASSIST EASTERN CANADIANS TO COPE WITH HIGH PRICES
speechtext: You have not got a policy.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: OIL-MEASURES TO ASSIST EASTERN CANADIANS TO COPE WITH HIGH PRICES
speechtext: George, I think you should go back to the time when you just contented yourself with looking like Gorgeous George.

subtopic: OIL-MEASURES TO ASSIST EASTERN CANADIANS TO COPE WITH HIGH PRICES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: OIL-MEASURES TO ASSIST EASTERN CANADIANS TO COPE WITH HIGH PRICES
speechtext: I am getting to him. The Prime Minister says, let them burn wood. That is his policy.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: OIL-MEASURES TO ASSIST EASTERN CANADIANS TO COPE WITH HIGH PRICES
speechtext: Order, please. Perhaps the Prime Minister might be allowed to repeat his reply. There are a few supplementaries by the hon. member for Central Nova and the hon. member for St. John's East. We will then try to move on.

subtopic: OIL-MEASURES TO ASSIST EASTERN CANADIANS TO COPE WITH HIGH PRICES
speechtext: I didn't know I could get under your skin so well.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: OIL-MEASURES TO ASSIST EASTERN CANADIANS TO COPE WITH HIGH PRICES
speechtext: The hon. member does not get under my skin with the knife he put under the skin of his former leader.

subtopic: OIL-MEASURES TO ASSIST EASTERN CANADIANS TO COPE WITH HIGH PRICES
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subtopic: OIL-MEASURES TO ASSIST EASTERN CANADIANS TO COPE WITH HIGH PRICES
speechtext: You are frightfully funny this morning. Let's get back now to your wood burning policy.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: OIL-MEASURES TO ASSIST EASTERN CANADIANS TO COPE WITH HIGH PRICES
speechtext:
I must repeat that I do not assume that the federal government must in every case subsidize citizens of some provinces when the provincial governments themselves have just received $190 million in equalization
December 14, 1973

funds over and above the amount received in previous years. They have received this as a result of a change in the equalization policy. I believe they have some responsibility toward their own citizens, and I am a little surprised that federal Members of Parliament sitting opposite have no more concern for the federal taxpayers than they do.

subtopic: OIL-MEASURES TO ASSIST EASTERN CANADIANS TO COPE WITH HIGH PRICES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: OIL-MEASURES TO ASSIST EASTERN CANADIANS TO COPE WITH HIGH PRICES
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subtopic: OIL-MEASURES TO ASSIST EASTERN CANADIANS TO COPE WITH HIGH PRICES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have what I hope is a reasonably non-argumentative supplementary for the right hon. gentleman. I am not suggesting to the Prime Minister that the federal government bear the entire responsibility, but I should like to ask him whether he is prepared to consider on a short-term basis a measure, for example, reducing to some extent the federal sales tax on gasoline, or something else to help us, because it was the neglect of this government to build a pipeline that put us into this position in the first place.

subtopic: OIL-MEASURES TO ASSIST EASTERN CANADIANS TO COPE WITH HIGH PRICES
speechtext: We suggested it four years ago, and you know it.

subtopic: OIL-MEASURES TO ASSIST EASTERN CANADIANS TO COPE WITH HIGH PRICES
speechtext: Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: OIL-MEASURES TO ASSIST EASTERN CANADIANS TO COPE WITH HIGH PRICES
speechtext: I certainly accept the representation made by the hon. member, but I put it to him and, indeed, to the provincial governments that they, too, might consider reducing their gasoline taxes.

subtopic: OIL-MEASURES TO ASSIST EASTERN CANADIANS TO COPE WITH HIGH PRICES
speechtext: And if they did, would you?

subtopic: OIL-MEASURES TO ASSIST EASTERN CANADIANS TO COPE WITH HIGH PRICES
speechtext: Give your backbenchers a chance.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: OIL-MEASURES TO ASSIST EASTERN CANADIANS TO COPE WITH HIGH PRICES
speechtext: Order, please. The Prime Minister might be allowed to reply to the question. There are a number of supplementaries. For the moment the Prime Minister has the floor.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: OIL-MEASURES TO ASSIST EASTERN CANADIANS TO COPE WITH HIGH PRICES
speechtext: This is the kind of subject we shall be discussing at the federal-provincial conference. I hope the provinces will come to that conference prepared to pay some money. The easy solution of equalization would mean we would take all the money from Alberta and redistribute it to the eastern provinces. I see the hon. member is shaking his head. I hope he and his friends will indicate whether they have some alternative approach which might be useful for the federal-provincial conference in January.

speakeroldname: Mr. dames A. McGrath (St. John's East):
subtopic: OIL-MEASURES TO ASSIST EASTERN CANADIANS TO COPE WITH HIGH PRICES
speechtext: In view of the fact the five eastern provinces have taxed their people to the limit of their capacity to pay and in view of the additional expenditures these provinces have to undertake because of excessively high unemployment, may I ask the Prime Minister whether he is prepared at the federal-provincial conference in January to increase equalization payments to these five provinces so they can reduce their taxes on gasoline?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: OIL-MEASURES TO ASSIST EASTERN CANADIANS TO COPE WITH HIGH PRICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the House should realize that as the revenues to Alberta go up because of eventual increases in the price of petroleum the consequences in regard to equalization payments will be of very great

magnitude, and that through the very operation of the equalization system these massive new revenues to Alberta will be redistributed through that system to the have-not provinces. This should be kept in mind by members over there who are always urging the federal government to place an even heavier burden upon federal taxpayers so as to help their own provinces. I must urge them to act as representatives of all Canadians and not only of one particular province.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: OIL-MEASURES TO ASSIST EASTERN CANADIANS TO COPE WITH HIGH PRICES
speechtext: Order, please. Perhaps we might have a last supplementary on this subject, after which I will see the hon. member for Fraser Valley West.

speechtext: The House resumed from Thursday, December 13, consideration of the motion of Mr. Macdonald (Rosedale) that Bill C-236, to provide a means to conserve the supplies of petroleum products within Canada during periods of national emergency caused by shortages or marked disturbances affecting the national security and welfare and the economic stability of Canada and to amend the National Energy Board Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on National Resources and Public Works.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ALLOCATION BOARD, MANDATORY ALLOCATION OF SUPPLIES AND RATIONING OF CONTROLLED PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last night when I called it ten o'clock I was commenting on how important historically and currently energy in the form of natural gas is to my constituency of Medicine Hat and in particular to the city of Medicine Hat. I had given some specific examples of what natural gas had done for my city, and I had concluded at ten o'clock by saying that all of Canada will benefit from the end product of this activity plus the export of surplus natural gas to central Canada. I added that it is not an exaggeration to suggest that both the city and the rural communities served by Medicine Hat and Redcliff have waited some 70 odd years for this pay off.
I want to give hon. members a personal glimpse of what energy means to me as a landowner. Thanks to the foresight of my grandfather and my father I have been most fortunate in that I presently own the mineral rights to a section of my cattle range. The deed or title to this land not only signifies my right to the surface, but with respect to the minerals under that surface it reads something like this, and I am paraphrasing here from memory. It gives me the rights to all mines and minerals except gold and silver which may be found to exist within upon, or under, and includes precious stones but excludes all coal, which is reserved for the Canadian Pacific Railway.
That is the way in which a deed reads in Alberta with respect to the mineral rights on lands which some of us who are fortunate still own. For 42 years, since our natural resources were returned to the province, mineral right taxes have been paid on this land just like the surface land tax, both payable to the government of Alberta.
There is a very important and fundamental issue at stake here that strikes at the very roots of private enterprise. This is a pillar of my own personal way of life. I refer to the fact, Mr. Speaker, that that land title gives me
December 14, 1973

the right to develop and produce agricultural products from the surface, and in addition I am entitled to the benefits of production from below the surface, subject only to the restrictions in the deed.
I say to this House that these fundamental rights of the individual, and indeed the rights of the province of Alberta, are in serious doubt due to the very far reaching and severely restrictive powers suggested in this energy allocation bill. Alberta's energy supplies allocation board will be acting as a Crown corporation and it will be their constitutional right to regulate energy production and price. This bill in many respects is somewhat comparable to the first C-176 bill of over two years ago, the federal farm products marketing bill, and is similar at least to the first drafts, with its very restrictive supply-management concepts. Bill C-236 provides for an allocation agency as powerful and far reaching as the wartime prices and trade board.
The supreme power of the minister under this bill surely must be subject to review and revision. The bill as proposed would allow for control of production and pricing of Medicine Hat's utilities that have been operating since 1900, including, of course, its electrical utility. Surely such a prospect will cause grave concern to Medicine Hat's industries and in particular to the new petrochemical industries.
In my opening remarks I went into some detail to point out the significance and importance of natural gas development to my riding. All of this development came about as a direct result of a free and private enterprise system. It should be noted that nearly all of the gas development has been done by that group generally known as the independent petroleum group, owned and controlled mainly by Canadians. This same development was possible because of the risk capital made available by the independents. It was made available, of course, in anticipation of reasonable profits. I say "reasonable" profits and not so-called "windfall" profits. This term, thanks to the NDP-Liberal coalition, is becoming almost as offensive in its connotations as the term "corporate ripoff".
I ask these questions, Mr. Speaker. Was it windfall profits from the United States that first supplied the risk capital to start Alberta's oil boom in pre-Leduc days? Was it windfall profits that helped develop the ranching industry at Walsh, with Sarnia Financing, for the Sarnia Ranching Company? Was it windfall profits that prompted the governor and company of adventurers of England trading into Hudson Bay to invest in the future of Northwest Canada 300 years ago? The same can be asked of the backers of the Northwest Company. Was it windfall profits from the United Kingdom and France that led to the early development of the New England states and French Canada? No one can properly describe the $90 million operational debt of great Canadian oil sands, over and above its capital costs, as windfall profits! In all these cases, of course, there was a genuine profit motive, but surely there was something more that can only be explained by the desire of enterprising men to accept a challenge to develop a new country such as Canada.
Energy Supplies Emergency Act
There are too many suggestions and insinuations these days that there is something immoral about making a profit. I for one will never be ashamed of any profits I make. And they have not been windfall profits. The cattle industry in western Canada for 20 years, from 1951 to 1971, was without adequate profits and very often incurred losses.
As one of Alberta's 19 members of parliament, I am sure I speak for my constituents when I say that we in the Medicine Hat constituency are very mindful and concerned about central and eastern Canada's energy distribution problem. We will willingly share our excess natural gas on a preferential basis with you, but do not ask us to do it as a handout, and do not ask us to allow the proceeds of the export tax to be used for this purpose. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) must be continually reminded of their statements in this House and to the media that the total proceeds of this tax will indeed go back to the province of origin.
In its present form, Mr. Speaker, I cannot support Bill C-236. This is not to say that there is not an energy problem, perhaps even a crisis, in Canada today. It is my personal opinion that there are enough federal government agencies right now to properly deal with the current situation. There were clear signs of this current energy situation long before we got into the heating months. The very important first ministers' conference called for next January should surely have been organized the day after the Middle East war began. Further to this bill, when it does go into committee, the highest priority must be given to a detailed and accurate accounting of our oil shortfall, if indeed there is one.
As I conclude these remarks, Mr. Speaker, I want to make it very clear that I am completely opposed to using taxpayers' money to buy or otherwise take over an existing oil company that was established within a competitive, private enterprise system. Nor can I see the current need for the creation of another Crown corporation as an alternative to a takeover of an oil company.
In most of our large scale Canadian developments we have had to rely on foreign investment to get the job done due to three basic considerations. First, as a young nation we simply did not have enough total dollars available. Second, after more dollars were available, for reasons that are somewhat obscure Canadians were not prepared to invest in their own country. Third, we did not have enough of our own know-how.
Today I suggest that the first and third considerations no longer exist. We do have the dollars and we do have the know-how. In particular, in Alberta we definitely have the know-how for oil and gas development. As to Canadians being ready to invest in Canada, perhaps this is the right time and opportunity to find out. Certainly Alberta found out some years ago that Albertans were more than willing to invest in their future when the Alberta gas trunk line was formed. I have every confidence as an Alberta citizen that there will be a rush to oversubscribe the new proposed Alberta energy company. If we must have a new Crown corporation for energy, why not a Canadian energy company without a single tax dollar in it? Why not give Canadians a chance to subscribe to it on a voluntary

December 14, 1973
Energy Supplies Emergency Act basis? The results could be surprising. Who knows, there might even be some windfall profits.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I cannot close these remarks without a comment on the recent personal attack on Alberta's first minister by Canada's Prime Minister. Prior to the Prime Minister's Vancouver speech, there were clear signs of a new co-operation beginning between Alberta and central and eastern Canada. Certainly there was a feeling that Ontario and Alberta were resolving their differences over natural gas supplies by quiet, behind-the-scenes discussions. The Prime Minister's ill tempered outburst against our Alberta premier sets a new low for federal-provincial diplomacy and indeed lends credence to the suggestion now prevalent that the government has written off Alberta politically.
I said earlier there can be no trade-off regarding the export tax remittance to the provinces. I say further that surely there can be no trade-off involving Alberta oil and the bilingual issue. The member for Edmonton-Strath-cona (Mr. Roche) was right on when he said last night in this debate that this is a government that uses, and abuses, national unity for its own political survival.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to take a few minutes to express one or two thoughts on the bill before us, to deal with some of its principles, and to comment on what is happening during this debate on this bill.
The bill proposes that, in light of the possibility of a genuine and serious energy crisis in this country, a crisis more serious than now, some authority shall be vested in the government-the authority is vested mainly in the government and not in the board-to allocate supplies of energy to regions and to activities which need it most and which are at the centre of Canadian life and welfare.
I emphasize that anyone who reads the bill carefully will see that it is not the board, really, which will have these powers. Any actions of the board are always to be subject to approval by the federal government. Frequently those actions are to be initiated by the governor in council. The government is responsible to parliament for any action it takes. Furthermore, if one reads the bill carefully, one will note that no allocation program can begin unless the conditions in Canada are such as to justify the government's declaring a national emergency.
The government seeks to take powers under this bill to do a number of things which are normally under provincial jurisdiction. In order, constitutionally, to be able to exercise those powers or, putting it more cautiously, in order to be able to make a case for exercising those powers, the government would declare a national emergency and rely on the peace, order and good government provision of the British North America Act. Therefore, the program of allocations cannot even start, and the regulations under the act can have no effect, unless the conditions with respect to energy in this country are so serious, so critical, that the government has reasons, which it can substantiate in court, for declaring a national emergency. That being so, I cannot understand some of the arguments

which have taken place, in view of the framework of this bill. I will return to that in a moment.
Certainly there is great need for clarification of a number of the proposals in the bill. Certainly there is great need for a number of amendments, because some of the powers are unnecessarily large or unnecessarily wide. There is need to amend the bill. There is therefore a need for the parliamentary committee to consider this bill as quickly as possible, since that is where the amendments can be brought forward.
Amendments cannot be brought forward in these generalized speeches in which we are now indulging on second reading. They cannot be brought forward so long as second reading is dragged out for some purpose that I cannot for the life of me understand. The actual, substantial changes to the bill can only be made in committee, once the bill is before the standing committee of parliament. There members can see if they can persuade each other to make changes for improving the bill, both as to the breadth of its powers and as to the way in which its provisions may function later. That is why I cannot for the life of me understand why the Conservative members have apparently taken the decision to drag out this debate on the bill.

This is the only piece of legislation before this parliament which gives somebody the power to allocate supplies to places that are most seriously in short supply. This legislation wants to make certain that people in areas of this country experiencing a particularly difficult energy situation may at least get some of the energy supplies they need in order to carry on their work and their lives. It would make certain that hospitals, schools, old age pensioners' homes and the like would get supplies that are available elsewhere in this country. This is the only piece of legislation which makes that possible.
As I said, it can and should be improved, and no doubt will be improved in committee. But it is perfectly obvious
December 14, 1973

that for some political reason that God alone knows- certainly I don't understand it-the shortsighted Conservative members in this House are going to prevent this bill from getting to committee where it might be improved, after which its provisions could become available to parts of the country which need assistance.
I can understand that the Conservative party might try to hold up something which deals with the export tax, which apparently it opposes, or the division of the income from the export tax, which it opposes. But why in the name of heaven should Conservative members hold up the only piece of legislation which may be of value to Quebec and the Atlantic provinces if those areas run into serious shortages of supply?
The only reason I can think of, Mr. Speaker, is that Conservative party members are so wedded to the idea that the oil corporations must not be interfered with under any circumstances that they are prepared to put Quebec and the Atlantic provinces in jeopardy by holding up this bill. If I am wrong about Conservative intentions, then I appeal to them to stop the filibuster on second reading. Let us get this bill to the committee. Let us work there to improve it, so that the powers are not broader than those needed and so that they may perform the functions that are intended. But for heaven's sake let us not put Quebec, eastern Canada and other parts of this country in even greater jeopardy by acting as irresponsibly as the Conservative members are acting.

As a member for Atlantic Canada I am naturally very concerned, not only about what is going to happen this winter, but what will happen in the days ahead. Our people are facing an energy crisis which has resulted from the decision that has been made by this government in so far as the supply of fuel is concerned for the people in that part of Canada.
I am very concerned about the attitude of the Prime Minister. Not very long ago he made a visit to Halifax to participate in a testimonial dinner given for the President of the Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen). It was a gala affair. At that time the Prime Minister cited some very pleasing examples of progress in that part of Canada in so far as regional economic disparity is concerned. He did not encounter any criticism from any member on this side of the House about the statistics he was placing before the people of Nova Scotia, because we recognize there has been some progress made through the Department of Regional Economic Expansion and other federal departments in producing equality of opportunity across this nation. While we did not argue the point, we believe progress could be made faster if some of the policies we

At the same time, in one fell swoop the Prime Minister allowed a policy to go into effect that will do much to eradicate the hard work that has been done by many dedicated people in the federal government, namely, allow an escalation of prices that our people are just not capable of handling.
On numerous occasions my leader has enunciated ways and means of eliminating this problem. The Prime Minister said we will remain at the mercy of the "Sheiks of Araby" as far as the prices of gasoline and home heating fuel are concerned. We in this party do not believe that is good government. The Prime Minister also said that because we enjoyed a lesser cost of petroleum products coming from offshore and, according to his estimate, have had a net dividend of some $500 million, we should not now complain because we have to pay $3 a barrel more for oil than other people in Canada. He forgets two things. First, in order for the poor governments of the Atlantic provinces to produce a highway system equivalent to the system across this country, it has had to tax our people a great more throughout that period of time.
When the Diefenbaker government was in office, assistance was provided to ensure that the trans-Canada highway was as good in Newfoundland as it was in British Columbia. But at no time did the users of petroleum in the maritime provinces enjoy supplies at a price lower than anybody else in Canada. In fact, they always paid more. And they paid more because taxes were higher. It was as simple as that.

From the primitive beginnings leading up to and forming our Canadian confederation, energy has been our chief concern and our chief servant. There is scarcely a waterfall with power potential in southern Canada that has not been harnessed in the past. I point out to the House that even our smaller rivers have been harnessed in the past to saw lumber and grind grain, though many of these flumes, penstocks and wheels have been abandoned. In a good many instances these waterfalls could be rejuvenated and restored in order to contribute a small, I admit, but appreciated supply of electric power in the future.

I can say to you and to the House, Mr. Speaker, with some measure of satisfaction and pride that this type of hydraulic energy and conservation put me into politics. Mr. Speaker, just before lunch I was talking about the need to conserve energy in order to contribute to the economic stability of Canada, and I was about to read a letter that I sent over ten years ago to the Atomic Energy Commission of Canada and to Ontario Hydro, aimed at that goal of bringing about better economic stability in Canada. At the time we thought that the generating station might take the form of a nuclear power station, but due to problems and difficulties in the 1960's with nuclear-powered stations the decision finally taken was to erect a thermal station using oil for fuel. The letter reads as follows:
Ottawa, Aug. 21, 1963
Dear Mr. Gray:
Pursuant to the appointment which you kindly granted me today, during which we discussed the merits, physical and geographical, of the constituency of Prince Edward-Lennox as the location for a Nuclear Power Thermo Electric Generating Station, I wish to outline the following points in favour of this area.
It is true that a site for a plant of this kind must have the following requisites:
(1)	A solid rock foundation of understratum not subject to seismic movement or disturbances of the earth.
(2)	A deep and limitless supply of cold clean water.
(3)	The site should be in a preferably undeveloped area, sufficiently isolated to be of a minimum hazard to persons and property, and in an area not likely to soon become crowded by urbanization.
(4)	The plant should be located where the Provincial and National power grid can be fed by the shortest possible transmission equipment from the plant to the point where it feeds the grid. This makes for maximum efficiency of transmission and minimizes the natural loss of voltage which increases in ratio to distance in the transmission of electricity.
(5)	Economically, it is well for a site of this kind to have a suitably developed and well serviced housing area in convenient and safe proximity. This dispenses with the necessity of Government or Hydro having to make huge investments in town-sites and services to accommodate their personnel.
Both Prince Edward and Lennox Counties possess all these vital requisites for a plant of this kind. May I point out to you that facing directly on Lake Ontario the Townships of Ameliasburg, Hillier, Hallowel, Athol, South Marysburg, North Marysburg, in Prince Edward County, and South Fredericksburg and Ernestown in the County of Lennox could all readily qualify to accommodate this type of utility. The location of the area as a whole is strategically sound, in that a transmission line from Prince Edward County would feed the power grid in the vicinity of Trenton which is less than 100 miles east of the boundaries of Metropolitan Toronto. If located on the Lennox shores of Lake Ontario, the plant would likely feed the power grid at, or near Napanee, which is only nine miles straight across country from the north shore of Lake Ontario.
Furthermore, it is my firm opinion that a generating plant in this area could most efficiently supply the ever-increasing needs of that fast-developing area of which it is a part, the diversified and productive triangle lying east of Toronto, south of the Ottawa, and north of the St. Lawrence River. I also point out to you that in this latter area, along the lakefront of South Fredericksburg and Ernestown Townships, we have ideal deep water facilities for the economic handling of fuel from large ships in case the generating station may take the form of a coal or oil fired installation rather than of nuclear power.
Energy Supplies Emergency Act
I thank you for your attention in this matter, confident that in the deliberations Atomic Energy of Canada Limited and Ontario Hydro will give all due consideration to my request that you explore the sound potentialities of Prince Edward-Lennox in your search for a proper site for this utility.
I am,
Yours respectfully, Douglas Alkenbrack, M.P. (Prince Edward-Lennox)
I thought the House would be interested in that letter since it resulted in a project that is certainly going to contribute to the economic stability of Canada, one of the subjects and purposes of this bill.
The date of that letter was August 21, 1963. In December, 1968 Ontario Hydro announced its intention to build the Lennox . generating station in South Fredericksburgh township, utilizing facilities conducive to economy of production of electrical energy from petroleum fuels.
This energy supply project is now well advanced in construction, with its 600-foot stack already a towering landmark in the Lennox countryside. As I said, this station will be oil-fired, using a bunker 6-C fuel, a residual oil which will come from Venezuela. This plant will be the most modern of its type. It has the largest oil storage in North America, three tanks 360 feet in diameter and 48 feet high, each of them larger than a football field. Each one of these tanks holds 833,000 barrels of oil. This plant at full load could burn 3,120 barrels per hour. Its four boilers each can produce 3,600,000 pounds of steam per hour, turning four turbine generators to provide a total capacity of 2,300,000 kilowatts.
