They should listen and take heed, because we are offering sound and sage advice to them on this serious matter. It is obvious that they have been getting very poor advice up to now, so they might as well sit and listen. If the energy minister decides that it is getting too hot in the kitchen and it is time to leave the House, I would remind him that it may be awfully cold in tens of thousands of kitchens throughout Canada this winter because of his bungling.
The government's answer to the problem is to ask for autocratic and dictatorial power to control the production and use of all energy in our country. I cannot accept this as an answer. This is the government's answer to our urging action to develop a national energy policy. This is the government's answer to a problem that developed in part because they had a majority in the past and exercised the very same powers they are now asking us to give them. They abused that authority in the past and there is every reason to believe that they will abuse it in the future. This power must be kept from them, Mr. Speaker. Let the government go back to the people and seek power through a majority. Let them go to the people and try to explain away their abuse of the power they once had, and let them explain away their bungling and incompetence.
I should like to deal specifically with a few clauses in this bill that I find particularly onerous, and then ask whether any responsible and thinking member of this house could accept this bill, whatever side of the House he or she might be sitting on. I will go so far as to throw a challenge, through Your Honour of course, to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. Will the minister tell us in a few words how this bill could possibly correct the situation that this government has allowed to happen?
Specifically, it has allowed the Canadian people to be caught unawares by a world-wide oil shortage, when we are a major oil-producing country.
Energy Supplies Emergency Act
Subclause (4) of clause 9 reads:
The Board and its members are exempt from liability for any act or thing done or omitted by the Board in good faith in the exercise or purported exercise of a duty or power under this Act.
That is nothing but dictatorial power. Although these powers are supposedly vested in the board, they are actually vested in the minister. The powers for which he asks in clause 9 (4) are extraordinary. All of us in this House know that no citizen or resident of Canada can be exempt from responsibility for acts committed or omitted, whether in a private, public or official capacity. The only exception is the Governor General of Canada.
What is the government afraid of? Does the government have plans for this board that it is afraid to tell us about until we have approved its formation? What does this board plan to do, that it should be afraid of being held to account for its actions? There is something awfully suspicious about this provision that would confer greater immunity on the board members than is conferred on judges, parliamentarians or even diplomats. Clause 10 provides that:
The Board shall act under the instructions of the Governor in Council and report to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources from time to time upon its activities under this Act.
This gives the government a cozy little closed type of blanket authority to act in any way it sees fit, and charge it all up to some real or imagined energy crisis, or any other crisis it chooses to blame. Why should this House grant such authority to any agency of government, Mr. Speaker? Why should this House grant such powers to an agency of the Crown, such as the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, when he has proved to be incapable of administering his portfolio in the past and present? I do not see how he could be expected automatically to become effective simply because we have granted him powers that no one else possesses in our country.
It is my view that, as a minority government, this present government has more cheek and arrogance than it exhibited even when it had a majority. I am really amazed that the NDP would go along with giving this government so much power, such potential to play partisan politics, when there is no possibility that the NDP will ever reap any benefits from such power. Surely they are not unaware of the contempt in which they are held by this government, which uses them so skilfully for its own purposes.
As one reads through this bill, Mr. Speaker, one can see that it is designed to give this new agency absolute control over every form of energy produced or imported into Canada. The bill gives the agency absolute control over energy accumulation, over storage, over the wholesaling and retailing of energy and over the bookkeeping employed by suppliers and sellers of energy. Actually, Mr. Speaker, it is just the sort of statism that the NDP would impose on the Canadian people and the Canadian economy. If we allow government to open the door as wide as would be the case if this bill becomes law, it will be the beginning of the end for our free enterprise system.
This bill provides, among other things, for a takeover by the government of every aspect of electric power in Canada. I do not want the government to have this power. I do not want them to be the sole arbiter in this area; the

December 14, 1973
Energy Supplies Emergency Act provinces ought to have a voice here. That is why I think we should wait until the federal-provincial conference is held in the near future. As I say, I would not want the government to have this power, any more than I would want it to have absolute power over fossil fuels.
While we are debating this bill, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) is trying very hard to make Premier Lougheed of Alberta the culprit in the energy crisis, in spite of the fact that the premier has done everything in his power to see that Alberta crude finds its way to eastern Canada. It is not Premier Lougheed's fault that the federal government did not ensure that the pipeline system in Canada was extended at least as far as Montreal. It is not the premier's fault if the federal government still does not know the extent of the energy crisis as far as Canada is concerned.
We know and the Prime Minister knows that it is the fault of the federal government that we are in our present predicament. The Prime Minister is trying to use the energy crisis for political purposes, and this is despicable. He is trying to divide the Conservative party in Alberta from the federal party by trying to convince people in the east that Alberta's government is unwilling to co-operate with the federal government in Ottawa.
Nothing could be further from the truth. I do not blame Premier Lougheed for refusing to let the federal government put him over a barrel, an oil barrel or any other kind. This government has to come up with a scapegoat every time it goofs or bungles, and that is very, very often. This government bungles so regularly that one could set a clock by them, so there is always the need for a scapegoat. I suggest to the energy minister that he might very well be the next scapegoat, simply because he was not able to pin the blame for the energy crisis on Premier Lougheed. The energy minister is handy to the boss very close at hand, and he has fumbled the ball so frequently that he is vulnerable. The minister must be aware that he would not be the first cabinet minister that the Prime Minister has used as a scapegoat to cover up his own miscalculations.
In conclusion, I suggest that the Prime Minister should desist from using the bilingualism issue every time he wants to defuse a potentially explosive situation in the country. I say to the Prime Minister that bilingualism is not more important to this country than oil, the economy and the use of our resources. His statements are beneath the dignity of parliament, and while we are all aware of the contempt he holds for parliament, it would be fitting if he would conceal his contempt for the remainder of the brief period he will be sitting on that side of the House. I suggest that he inflict his spite on his ministers instead of this House and certain regions of this country. Rest assured, Mr. Speaker, the institution of parliament will outlive the present Prime Minister by a very long time.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak in this debate we must acknowledge the fact that the minister in charge of energy for Canada has been attempting for at least the past four months to create a feeling of crisis within Canada on the energy question. At times it appeared as though he had succeeded. Oil was found. Supplies kept coming into Canada. As the issue

became more clear in the minds of Canadians, we realized how fortunate we are that we do not yet have an oil crisis.
There is no question but that there is a crisis in the world. The Americans are in trouble. Europe is in trouble. Japan has been in trouble. We must analyse whether we have been using the right methods to meet a crisis if it should develop in Canada.
I have a copy of a daily oil news analysis which was published in New York. It is dated November 8, 1973. I will quote from it to give members an idea of what we are doing. This talks about Calgary and the western Canadian based oil industry that exists. I quote:
Its 275 companies, from the big subsidiaries of U.S. majors to small independents, have become helpless pawns in the fast-deteriorating energy chess game between Alberta and the Canadian federal Government.
In recent days Saskatchewan got involved in that chess game. We welcome her concern and participation.
Why did the government attempt to create a crisis long before it was necessary? I think this stems from their position in the House of Commons, a very minority position. They failed to gather appeal across the country so attempted to create an issue in the hope they could go to the country and win an election on some short-term policy they had devised. A week ago last Thursday some people thought that going to the country was what we might be doing. However, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) made a speech in which he attempted to lure the NDP vote. Many right-wing members within his party must have been saddened and shocked by his brazen courting of the socialist philosophy. If they had thought back awhile, they would not have been shocked. They would have realized these were the true colours coming out.
I have an editorial which appeared in the December 8 edition of the Albertan. The writer was referring to the courting and marriage that took place a week ago Thursday. It reads in part:
Socialists for years
Over a period of four years or more I have attempted, quite unsuccessfully it is true, to prepare my readers for the federal government's ultimate move toward socialism. The facts were all there for everyone to see.
Let us go over them again, just briefly. Before the "Three Musketeers" who are the guiding lights of the federal government at Ottawa, Trudeau, Marchand and Pelletier, entered federal politics, they were mouthpieces of the socialist party in Quebec. They campaigned, wrote and distributed pamphlets in behalf of the NDP and it was not until the people of Quebec demonstrated in no uncertain terms that they wanted nothing to do with socialism as a political way of life, that they turned their coats and joined the Liberal party.
The right-wing Liberals succumbed and allowed these men to lead their party. We all remember the leadership convention at which time the Prime Minister took over the party. It should not be a surprise to the free enterprise people within the Liberal party that these thoughts, deep concerns and true feelings have been there for a long time.
What is involved in this bill? It is a reach for power, dictatorial power, power which only a real socialist would love, power which only a real socialist could appreciate, power to take away the freedom of the individual.

speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board
speechtext:
Price and wage control?
December 14, 1973
Price and wage control would be nothing compared to the rationing and complete control that this bill could bring about.
Hear, hear!

We have had a bit of a rift with the United States over this problem. In their energy crisis, their leader stated quite clearly that by the end of this decade they will have developed the potential to meet their own energy needs without depending on any foreign nation. That is what Mr. Nixon said recently with regard to their energy crisis.
What was being said in the United States in 1969 with regard to the energy crisis? Late in 1969, the United States cabinet report on energy future recommended closer relations with Canada on energy, but suggested that Canada could only be counted upon as a secure source of oil if it took steps to reduce the then total dependence of Quebec and the Maritimes on overseas imports. At that time the United States saw the danger to Canada by taking cheap oil from what might be called an insecure source and doing very little about it.
Was the oil industry of Canada asleep at that time? No, not so. The Canadian independents under the IPEC association discussed the problem with the Prime Minister. He said "Go peddle your oil somewhere else. We do not want it. It is too expensive in the province of Quebec, especially the Montreal market." That is what he said in 1969.
Now, sad but true, we have before us what is called an allocations bill. It is going to set up an energy supply allocations board. The board may control not only products so designated by the Governor in Council, such as petroleum, hydrocarbons, electricity, but even products manufactured from petroleum, according to clause 12(5). The order of the Governor in Council may designate any products manufactured wholly or in part from petroleum or hydrocarbons and bring them under the allocation program.
What will the allocation board do? How much oil will it be able to divert to the five eastern provinces? I suppose that in theory it could divert as much oil as those provinces need. But the board could do this effectively only if transportation was available. I do not know how many members saw the article in the Financial Post last week. It described the idea of moving large amounts of oil by rail as pure fantasy, not because the railroads do not have the tracks, but because they do not have the tank cars. Spokesmen for the railway companies have themselves stated before the transport committee that the railways do not own any tank cars, they rent them. The tank car rental companies say there are no more of them available for hire, so it would be impossible to move by rail the 50,000 barrels a day to which the minister has referred from time to time.
Oil is moving to Vancouver right now through the Trans-Mountain pipeline. From there it is being taken by tanker down the coast and through the Panama Canal to eastern Canada. Loading facilities are such that at best it is not possible to deliver more than 70,000 or 75,000 barrels a day to that market. Sad as it may be, the facilities for
Energy Supplies Emergency Act doing better are not there. They will have to be built. So what will the allocation board really be doing?
How necessary is this board? A meeting of provincial first ministers is to take place in January, and the government, presumably with the idea of promoting a feeling of goodwill among the first ministers when they attend that meeting, wishes to confront them with a bill which has already been passed by this House. Are there no clauses in this bill which are negotiable with the premiers? This has been the trouble about the chess game we have been watching. The federal government has made up its mind as to its intentions and said ho-hum to the provinces and their desires. Is this a fair attitude to take if the first ministers' conference is to be carried on in a proper spirit so as to devise ways of meeting the energy crisis which could develop in Canada should the Arabs shut off the oil being delivered to the five eastern provinces?
Richard Gwyn, a civil servant for some time, now writing for the Toronto Star, had this to say on December 8:
Lougheed, if he wants to do it all by himself, might, at least constitutionally, just be able to do so. His new marketing board will control all of Alberta's production and can determine to whom it sells and at what prices.
So we are headed toward a direct confrontation. About a month ago someone asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to remove the present minister of energy from office and give him the job of House leader again.
A Senate seat.

That is a good suggestion. He would be the greatest confrontationist the Senate has ever seen. He might liven that place up a great deal. But to send the present minister out to a conference which is headed toward confrontation, taking with him legislation which has already been passed, committing him to an inflexible position, is surely no way to create a proper spirit among the ten ministers who will be present. Mr. Gwyn goes on in this article to say:
The constitution gives Ottawa jurisdiction over interprovincial trade. But Alberta may have more scope than at first seemed likely. Alberta owns its oil in the literal sense of the word: it comes from Crown lands leased but not sold to the oil companies.
I wish to emphasize that last sentence, particularly for the benefit of hon. members who sit on my left. It is not the terrible multinational oil companies who own this oil but the government of Alberta, according to Mr. Gwyn, and I am inclined to agree with him. This article is one which is well worth reading. It suggests that passing the bill before us would do nothing to create harmony among the ministers attending the conference; rather, it would interfere with the goodwill necessary if we are to meet the difficult situation which may develop in the coming winter.
The Globe and Mail of November 30 carried an article under the heading "Saskatchewan orders cutback in oil output." It states;
A spokesman for the mineral resources department said in an interview that the government had sent letters to oil companies ordering a 16 per cent cutback in production in southeast Saskatchewan (9,300 barrels a day) and a 40 per cent reduction in southwest Saskatchewan (26,200 barrels) for December.

December 14, 1973
Energy Supplies Emergency Act
Well, Saskatchewan can do this if it wishes, I suppose, but it suggests to me that the province is getting its back up and is fed up with the confrontation tactics of the federal energy minister. It seems Saskatchewan, too, wants to go to this conference with its mind firmly made up, not prepared to give away very much.
Since that article appeared Saskatchewan, as is well known, has brought in legislation making it plain that by January 1 they will be putting on their own tax of $2.20 a barrel. This will lead automatically to an increase in the price of crude oil in eastern Canada, or at least an increase in the price of that proportion of the market which Saskatchewan supplies, amounting to about 25 per cent of the oil consumed in Ontario.
I do not know what the leader of the New Democratic Party thinks about that, but here again a province is declaring, well in advance of the forthcoming conference, how it intends to act. It is headed foi confrontation, particularly if we as legislators in this parliament do not caution the government and make it clear that the allocation bill we are being asked to pass represents a reach for power not granted to any federal government except in time of war. It is an encroachment upon provincial rights.
I know there are few, if any, members of a provincial government who would agree with the terms of clause 14, which states:
Where it is considered necessary to do so for the purpose of conserving the available supplies of such petroleum products as have been included in a mandatory allocation program, the Governor in Council may amend the mandatory allocation program by adding electric power thereto and establishing mandatory allocation thereof.
This is bound to upset the provinces, especially if this clause is approved by the House before the conference is due to begin. Many people in central Canada have looked upon Alberta as being anti-Prime Minister, and in his speech in Vancouver the Prime Minister attempted to paint a picture of this terrible premier from Alberta and how he has tried to hold up the consumers in the rest of Canada.
Right.

Some hon. members over there says "right". Let me explain Alberta's position. Alberta has passed and is passing legislation, but it has not said it is going to implement a tax, such as Saskatchewan has, by January 1. Alberta has not cut back on production. In fact, since this crisis became obvious Alberta has increased production to a small extent, in fact to the extent that the transportation facilities could move the products to eastern Canada.
As early as October 29, or perhaps as late as November 29, Alberta laid down a five-point program in which it outlined its oil problems. In the preamble of that five-point program Alberta acknowledges ownership of 85 per cent of the petroleum resources now found in Canada and the fact that it is producing 80 per cent of Canadian production, probably supplying over 50 per cent of Canada's needs at this time.

This five-point program points out what Alberta believes should be its policy, and it is interesting to note that security of supply for Canadians is the number one point on that list. That does not suggest to me that Premier Lougheed is a wild, blue-eyed Arab out to rob the rest of Canada. Security of supply for Canadians is the first point in that policy, and this is a point which was amply demonstrated and should have been apparent as early as 1969.
I will not read the details of each of these points, merely the headings. The second point relates to a fair return for Alberta's resources. The premier does not suggest he wants pie in the sky, but he does want a fair return for Alberta's diminishing resources. What kind of a premier would he be if he did not want that, and what kind of respect would the Alberta voters have for him if he turned over the stewardship for Alberta resources to someone who did not want a fair return? I suggest that any individual in this House, were he premier out there, would ask for the same thing. That is not out of the way at all.
Number three relates to a price for petroleum products for the Canadian consumer. The premier is not suggesting he wants the world price for the Canadian consumer, but he is in fact prepared to negotiate a price.
Number four deals with provincial responsibility for a resource policy. We are living in a federal society under a federal system, and our constitution lays down the fact that the provinces have a responsibility for resources. Section 109 of the British North America Act provides for provincial ownership of mineral resources, and this was part of the making of this country of ours when it was put together under the British North America Act. This may have been a mistake, but we came together with that provision. What kind of a government do we have here that wants unilaterally to break that provision? I am not suggesting that Lougheed will not allow some changes, but I am saying that this government through this Bill C-236 wants unilaterally to break that agreement which eventually brought 10 provinces together to make this country of Canada. We have heard a lot of talk about the fact that this Prime Minister is the one who wants to keep Canada together. He has not suggested that lately, because if he did no one would believe him.
The fifth point in the Alberta oil policy relates to investment opportunities for Canadians. We have heard much said about the profits of multinational oil companies, and about the Ottawa Valley line established by the former Conservative government in 1961. This line was established to encourage Canadian investment in the oil industry and increased production from oil wells in Alberta. At the time these wells were producing at less than 50 per cent capacity. Many of the smaller Canadian-owned companies could not survive with that low production as they did not have the cash flow. There had to be increased demands in order to make sure that these wells were economical and producing more profit. These increased demands have been beneficial to all Canada, as has been proven, and the situation will be even further improved in the next 10 years if everyone adopts the attitude of negotiation rather than demand.
There is no question that during the 10 years leading up to 1961, or even during the seven years from 1954 to 1961,
December 14, 1973

many small oil companies in western Canada were bought up by or amalgamated with the larger companies because they could not exist with the low cash position they were in as a result of cutbacks in production. This created a situation in which some of the larger international oil companies with huge financial reserves were able to get a hold on the oil industry.
I might point out that even today, as a result of government interference, oil shares on the stock market have been dropping rather than going up, even though prices have been going up and profits have been increasing. When the big oil companies begin to pull out of Canada we will find there is no confidence in the industry, and we cannot expect in that environment that small companies and individual Canadians will plough their money back into that resource. The Prime Minister sort of recognized this when he said in his great speech on Thursday that we are going to create a national oil company. That was very interesting and a lot of people perked up their ears. Members of the NDP to my immediate left pounded their desks because they thought we were on the right road to somewhere.
What have we heard about this company since last Thursday? We have heard it is going to spend $40 million almost immediately on research in developing the tar sands. The Syncrude project has not even started work yet. It has spent over $80 million on research but hopes to get started early next year.
$40 million over five years.

Someone suggests that the $40 million is to be spent over five years. That shows how much knowledge and interest the Prime Minister has really expressed about this matter. His lack of knowledge and interest was demonstrated last Wednesday as a result of some of his flippant replies to serious questions posed by members on this side of the House. I suggest he has no interest in hardly anything other than the promotion of the French language in Canada. That is about the extent of his interest.
And he is doing a lousy job of that.

To suggest that the Quebec people would rather have their own language promoted than buy one gallon of Alberta oil is to insult the intelligence and the broadmindedness of the Quebec people, and I hope the Prime Minister lives to regret that remark.
Einstein once said that nationalism is an infantile disease of mankind. With the world becoming smaller because of improved efficiency in transportation and communication, and as we become more knowledgeable of various people throughout the world, that statement of Einstein's, if it was true at the time he made it, certainly is true today.
We should not be afraid of foreign investment. We should have confidence in ourselves and a belief that we can control foreign investment. One wonders, when one looks at this bill and sees the clauses in it, specifically clause 19 which provides that the board will have power to
Energy Supplies Emergency Act ration, how rationing in Toronto will help us to get more oil into the Montreal market. How will rationing in Calgary help us to get more oil into the Maritimes market? It cannot. It might be an expression of the philosophy that we should all suffer a little together, but this will not help.
We have the reply of the Prime Minister to questions put to him by the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay). Last Wednesday the hon. member for Central Nova asked a legitimate question, namely, what the government intends to do about oil prices if they become so high that they will be practically prohibitive in the Atlantic provinces. The Prime Minister replied that if they become too high, people do not have to buy the oil. Was that a serious, sensible, conscientious remark for the Prime Minister of this country to make? It certainly was not. Was he concerned about the people in Nova Scotia, the people in Prince Edward Island or the people in Quebec? He certainly was not. What is the purpose of this bill if the government does not have a contingency plan to offset some extremely high prices that might be demanded in the five eastern provinces? What is the use of setting up this allocation board?
Some time ago, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) thought that the establishment of this board would assist the government in controlling the ships and in transporting oil via the Panama Canal. It will certainly not load the ships any faster. The loading facilities are being used to the utmost right now in the port of Vancouver and the most that they can get through the port is 75,000 to 80,000 barrels a day. So what will this allocation board do? It will add to the scare crisis in Canada. It will create in certain areas, if it is politically wise to create them, certain hardships because the government wants the country to feel there is a crisis at hand and the knight on a white charger rides to the rescue of the people of Canada. This is the situation they are trying to create. Last Wednesday the Prime Minister did not suggest, in his answer to the hon. member for Central Nova, that he had as yet found the horse on which to ride. He did not see the allocation bill as the horse on which he could ride to the rescue. All he said was that if prices became too high people should not buy.
It seems to me that if this government wants to barter in good faith it should not ask the House to pass this bill, nor should it attempt to have us pass the tax bill which may come up next week. It is all right for the House to debate these bills and to listen to the views of hon. members because the thinking and contributions of hon. members should be made known before the first ministers conference is held. In this way confrontation, which is already taking place between this government and Saskatchewan regarding the cutback in production in that province and the imposition of the tax as of January 31, will be avoided. But if parliament passes these two bills the government will be asking for confrontation; and have we not had enough of that kind of confrontation diplomacy so far between the ten provinces and the federal government, a diplomacy which was originated by the minister?
There are many people who blame the Arabs and claim that all the problems which may face Canada in the future can be laid solely at the door of the Middle East countries. That is not quite so. We know that 30 per cent of the oil

December 14, 1973
Energy Supplies Emergency Act imported by the five eastern provinces comes from the Arab countries. Most of it comes from Venezuela and what might be called OPEC.
Thirty per cent is an important amount.

I am glad the hon. member says that. It amounts to 200,000 barrels a day more or less. We in the province of Alberta have done our utmost, as I said, to continue to increase our production and to meet whatever solutions the transportation industry can offer to move oil into the Montreal market or into the five eastern provinces by boat or by rail. Production might go up to 100,000 barrels a day. It would be oil from the west going to where it has never gone before, namely, the five eastern provinces. Saudi Arabia has cut Canada right off. The minister does not want to acknowledge that fact, but it came out the other day. His classmate exposed him. I should like to see his classmate expose him a little more, because then perhaps the Prime Minister may take an increased interest in the energy crisis and in finding ways to solve it. Perhaps the 70,000 or 80,000 barrels a day which we may be short if every Arab country cuts us off can be made up with increased purchases from OPEC.
I think that one should point out the difficulties in which the Arab nations find themselves. I know from a fairly reliable source that in recent years the North American continent has increased its oil consumption by 6 per cent a year and Europe has increased its oil consumption by about 12 per cent a year. In order to meet these increases the Arab nations would have to increase their production by 30 per cent a year. Let us leave aside for a moment the war in the Middle East and consider what country would not be a little concerned in those circumstances. The Arab countries are aware of their known resources. They see their production having to be increased by 30 per cent a year to meet the demand. What country, in those circumstances, would not say to itself that maybe they should be charging a little more for their oil, maybe they have something that will run out and perhaps they should be getting a higher price to provide a better livelihood for their citizens in the years ahead? Canada is fortunate in this respect; we can become self-sufficient.
We are.

Yes, we are self-sufficient and we can provide all parts of Canada with oil. But there are two things that all parts of Canada must recognize. First of all, the five eastern provinces have got to say, "All right. We are prepared to take Canadian oil, and if necessary we are prepared to pay a little more for it in the years ahead because we understand the cost of producing oil in Canada is higher than it is in the Middle East." That is an important recognition which they must make. They have to recognize this before Canadian oil is forced upon them as a consequence of this allocation bill.
At the January conference of first ministers held in western Canada, in Toronto or in Ottawa, wherever it may be, they have to say publicly, "We will take this Syncrude oil, this Athabasca tar sands oil. We realize it costs more to

produce it, but we will take it even if other major pools of oil are found somewhere else." That is one thing they have to say very clearly and succinctly.
Why should private enterprise build a pipeline to Montreal just on a whim? Because the Arabs today are charging more for their oil, does this mean that forever and a day they will charge more for it? Private enterprise needs some assurance that the five eastern provinces recognize the venture they are entering upon with this oil arrangement.
The second thing that must be pointed out quite clearly is that repeatedly the province of Alberta has welcomed investment in the oil industry. We have not stopped investment money from coming into that province. Maybe we should have done so. Maybe we should say that while we know those tar sands have been there for 200 years, in another 200 years from now they will be even more valuable. But we have not said that. We have said to the province of Quebec that we do not think enough money is coming into the development of the tar sands. We welcome the creation of a corporation by the province of Quebec to spend money in assisting to develop the tar sands. We welcome a joint venture by both Quebec and Ontario, and the Alberta government itself is ready to take part in that venture.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. I regret to interrupt the hon. member, but his time has expired.
Mr. Speaker, may I have unanimous consent to express my final point?

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Does the House give unanimous consent?
Agreed.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I assure the House that I will not abuse the privilege it has granted me. As I was saying, we in Alberta welcome such investment to help meet the crisis that may develop in Canada, and we will invest in that venture ourselves so that we may better assist Canada in the years ahead. We have extended an invitation to a Crown corporation or a provincial corporation, and have even gone so far as to say that in order to encourage others the province of Alberta will go in as a part-owner of the corporation.
Having said that, I would refer to the five points that Premier Lougheed announced as our energy policy in the province of Alberta. Clearly we have invited foreign money. We have invited provincial money. We have invited Crown corporations to invest, purely in the interests of stepping up production. We have assisted in supplying oil to the five eastern provinces by shipping it through the Panama Canal. We have encouraged as much oil to be moved by rail into the Montreal market as is possible. No one in this House, or anywhere else, can say conscientiously and knowledgeably that the province of Alberta and its premier have not done their utmost to ward off any crisis which may be on the horizon. But if this House passes this bill before the first ministers' conference is held in January, few people in the House or in the cabinet will be able to say as much for the federal government.
December 14, 1973

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to have the opportunity to make a few comments on Bill C-236 concerning the government's plans to cope with the energy situation in our country. I think it is fair to say that the history of Liberal governments in this country has been of reaction to one crisis after another. Today we have a repetition of that history: things are no different. The government did not engage in the kind of medium or long-term planning that was necessary some time ago and again we are faced with a reaction to a crisis.
Policies on inflation, difficult as they may be to identify, have been one example of a panic and patchwork reaction designed to smooth things over but not to get at the basic cause of the problem. Now we have a policy on energy which also has been created in a panic situation but certainly is not designed to smooth things over. As a matter of fact, it seems designed to strain confederation to the limit.
We have seen the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and several other ministers making paradoxical policy statements and then putting forward policies that do not accord with their statements. In the past few days the Prime Minister and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) have placed a great deal of emphasis on the fact that they have frozen the price of oil, that controls have been placed on oil. This is a big thing to them. Yet at the same time we have the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) indicating on many occasions, including as recently as yesterday, that controls do not work, particularly when you have a shortage of supply. He believes the problem in that situation must be solved by increasing the supply. Yet what have we seen in the past few months? We have seen controls placed on meat to depress the price, controls on wheat used domestically to reduce its costs, and now controls on the price of oil.
I do not think anybody around here questions that so far as the world situation is concerned there is a shortage of oil. On the other hand, we have a Minister of Finance who says that in a shortage of supply situation controls do not work. Immediately following that we have the Prime Minister and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources placing price controls on that commodity. It is no wonder the Canadian public is confused on where the government stands. Are the people to believe the Prime Minister, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, or the Minister of Finance? Which of them is speaking the truth?
More basically, Mr. Speaker, we have in Canada today a government which appears to be more concerned with just surviving than with the realities of governing the country. The policies announced to deal with the energy crisis are good evidence of its desire to cling to power. Obviously some of them were taken from the NDP shopping list prepared just a few days ago. They were grasped greedily by the government in order to save itself. It is obvious that the government has been so preoccupied with the political survival game that it has been unable to govern at all. Recently I read an article quoting a Liberal source as saying that the Liberal Party, since its setback in October, 1972, has been unable to regain control of itself, has been unable to return to "its former grace." In fact, the Liberal Party seems to have entered the menopause, says this Liberal source. I think that Liberal source was rather
Energy Supplies Emergency Act generous when he suggested they were only in the menopause. If we examine the evidence more carefully, it points much more toward senility. One of the key features of senility is that individuals who suffer from it like to dwell on the distant past and do not like to look to the future because it appears rather bleak. If you examine statements made by ministers and members of the Liberal Party in recent weeks, you will find they have dwelt almost exclusively on past achievements and glories.
The speech made by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) on September 6 was entirely devoted to telling us how much the Liberal Party had done for Canada in the area of welfare in the last few years, typifying his preoccupation with the past, a typical symptom of senility. In the speech made by the Minister of State responsible for multiculturalism (Mr. Haidasz) a few months ago when this subject was before the House, he spent almost his entire time dwelling on past achievements. Most of his speech was about old history and the glory that used to be of the Liberal Party. If we look at some of the speeches made in recent weeks by the hon. member for Verdun (Mr. Mackasey) we find that he dwelt a good deal on past glories and not too much on the present or the future. When the Minister of Finance speaks he does the same thing, he always reviews old history. All these are examples of a party not in menopause but far beyond the menopause, well advanced into a state of senility.
I have also seen a report recently about the need of the Liberal Party to regenerate, suggesting it was shattered by the last election and has been unable to pull itself together to regenerate to a position of positive leadership. The word regenerate caught my eye because there are only a few creatures on this earth that can regenerate. I am told that if a spider loses a leg or a portion of it, it can regenerate or grow a new part. I am also told there is a certain kind of garden worm which, if you are digging and cut it in half with a shovel, will grow a new head section and a new tail section, so that what was originally one worm may wind up as two worms.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure that if you consider these remarks carefully you will see they are related to the bill before us. I am just trying to set the framework for my discussion. It would appear that in the last election the Liberal Party was cut in half by the spade of public opinion. I have had much difficulty trying to decide which section is here, whether it is the tail section or the head section that is trying to govern. I think it is probably the tail section. Looking at the energy policies that have been presented to us in the past few months, and at the statement on energy made about a week ago, one must come to the conclusion that it is the tail section of the worm that is governing and trying desperately to grow a new head section, but it appears unable to do so and from time to

Energy Supplies Emergency Act time it fits on the NDP head section as a substitute. Of course, that does not work because the NDP worm has been squirming so much that no one knows what path it wants to follow in what direction it wants to go.
It is waffling.

We have the spectacle of a party desperately clinging to power, improvising madly to provide symptomatic treatment for the ills of society but failing to come to grips with the cause of the problem, and therefore not providing the right prescription when it is required- and that is before the crisis occurs, not after. I think when a government deteriorates to the point where it appears to be completely incapable or unwilling to face squarely the problems of the country and provide the solutions which are bold and imaginative and which Canadians expect, it should step aside for the good of the country. When a government is as indecisive as this one has been, it should retreat into a cave to reassess its position; but in the meantime it should allow someone else to do the job, someone who is better suited and better prepared to do it.
The government claims that there is an energy crisis in Canada. No one questions the existence of a world shortage of energy or a world crisis, but we have yet to see the evidence that there is a crisis as far as this country is concerned. A few days ago the minister stated that under the worst circumstances Canada could be as much as 200,000 barrels a day short of oil this winter, but he has consistently refused or has been unable to provide any substantial evidence that there is in fact a shortage now or that there will be in fact a shortage this winter. Just a couple of days ago it was brought to our attention in the House that a couple of million barrels were being shipped out of Quebec to the United States under permit of the National Energy Board. That leads one to wonder how great a shortage there is of this product.
The minister himself indicates that an additional 100,000 barrels a day could be transported to Quebec and the maritimes from the west by way of tankers through the Panama Canal, down the St. Lawrence Seaway and by train and truck and every other means available. Recently we learned that a refinery at Come-By-Chance, Newfoundland, will be in production in the next month or so, producing an additional 100,000 barrels a day which are not committed to any market and are available to Canada.
Even under the worst possible conditions, in view of these facts and in view of the minister's projections, it is difficult to believe that there is indeed a crisis in Canada at this time. Nevertheless, the minister has placed Bill C-236 before the House and it is presently being debated. The bill gives the minister absolute power in the energy field to allocate energy supplies when he thinks economic conditions warrant the use of such power. Inasmuch as the industrial, commercial and business sectors of the economy depend upon energy to produce output, mandatory allocation and rationing of energy and energy products will give the minister complete authority to regulate the domestic economy as he sees fit.
I am not sure that I would be prepared to give this minister that kind of authority, Mr. Speaker. It would be a blatant distortion of the intent of this bill if it were openly to be used as an instrument of economic policy. But one

cannot assume that the government would not use such power as this bill provides if the government judged it politically expedient to do so. We have seen examples of government action for expediency in the past, and I am sure we will see such examples in the future. The economic powers that this bill provides cannot be underestimated. The allocation program itself can be invoked when in the opinion of the governor in council the stability of the economy is in danger because of a petroleum shortage or market dislocation.
What about the stability of the economy? I think, Mr. Speaker, that is very much a matter of opinion-presumably the opinion of the governor in council, which in fact means the opinion of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. On this matter his opinion should be identical with that of the Minister of Finance who has stated that a real growth rate of over 5 per cent is still expected in 1974.
The fact that mandatory allocations may be necessary probably means that growth projections are overly optimistic and probably not valid. It would be necessary for these optimistic forecasts for growth to be withdrawn in order to invoke the full powers of the energy allocation bill. Such withdrawal is not likely, particularly in view of the statement made yesterday by the Minister of Finance who spoke in the House in glowing terms about the expectations for economic growth. Also, the Prime Minister told the people of Canada last night that the predictions are for tremendous growth in this country in the next three years, for growth greater than in any other country of the world. So we are left wondering why this kind of allocation bill is required, if it is correct to assume that such growth will occur.
It is quite conceivable that a similar difficulty exists with regard to the opinion of what may be causing economic instability. For instance, the minister may use economic instability as an argument for invoking the powers under this bill. What are the causes of economic instability? They might be large increases in unemployment, not necessarily related to the energy crisis; they could be inflation and spiralling prices which have been completely out of control for months. The causes could be industrial shutdowns through lack of markets, or a general decline in investor confidence. None of these causes necessarily reflects the energy shortage. Equally, this manifest instability could be the result of other factors, such as mismanagement of monetary policy or the result of declining export markets. Therefore, the power which this bill provides for the minister to invoke allocations of energy could well be used as a disguise for the failure of the government's economic policies in general.
We are, however, prepared to accept for the time being the minister's word that there could be an energy shortage-
I don't know why.

I don't know why, either, but we are prepared to accept some legislative authority for coping with the situation, if it arises. However, this bill goes far beyond any conceivable need for power which the minis-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: Tory times are hard times.

We happen to be in the middle of Liberal times, and they are pretty hard times. Actually, some of the powers in this bill are so far reaching that the federal government could invade areas of undisputed provincial authority. In the past few weeks we have seen a deliberate attempt to run roughshod over provincial rights. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and the Prime Minister have engaged in confrontation with the producing provinces. For example, in Vancouver the Prime Minister a few days ago at a Liberal fund-raising dinner unashamedly attacked the premier of a province without any justification and without any regard for what that attack might do to confederation. We also saw the spectacle of the party to my left jumping for joy because the Liberals, with whom they are in cahoots, a few days ago put forward a policy which they support. Suddenly they were confounded when one of their own kind, the Premier of Saskatchewan, announced certain things that he wants to do for his province.
The hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) has been most critical of Alberta for wanting a good price for its product and some quid pro quo from the government. In other words, in exchange for better prices for Canadians that province wants certain things which it needs. The hon. member for York South thought that was terrible. He referred to the Alberta premier as a blue-eyed Arab. Now, suddenly, we have another blue-eyed Arab. Perhaps I should not say that. But the duly elected Premier of Saskatchewan is making demands which are far greater than those made by the Premier of Alberta. Suddenly, NDP members from Saskatchewan have been stopped in their tracks, wondering what to do now. What will they do now, I wonder? Will they support federal policies which would mean a loss of half a million dollars a day to the province of Saskatchewan, or will they reassess their position and decide on which side their bread is really buttered?
The confrontations which the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and the Prime Minister have provoked with the provinces have surprised me, as they have followed so closely on the heels of the western economic opportunities conference. If you recall, Mr. Speaker, prior to this conference the Prime Minister and the cabinet stirred up the fondest hopes of westerners that finally the government was taking a serious look at the west, was willing to listen to the problems of the west and, in fact, appeared to be
Energy Supplies Emergency Act willing to do something about those problems. Now the situation is quite different. We know where this Liberal government really stands so far as the west is concerned. Make no mistake, westerners get the message fully. The Prime Minister has decided to abandon the west, politically, and to go for broke in Ontario. I do not think the people of Ontario or the people of Canada can be fooled by this kind of attack on confederation. I would advise him strongly, as would other members of the opposition, to withdraw from that attitude.
What about my friends to our left, the great principled New Democratic Party which has been supporting this government unreservedly since January of this year? No matter what the issue has been, no matter what the position of the NDP has been prior to any vote, that party has repeatedly and consistently supported the government in order to stay alive itself. Last Monday it supported the government's energy policy. Now there is certain news from Saskatchewan and I am anxious to see what that party will do after today. Last summer, just after the parliamentary recess, the leader of the NDP went roaring from coast to coast saying, "I cannot see how we can support the Trudeau government much longer," knowing full well that there would not be any opportunity to carry out his threat by way of a vote until the middle of October. Then, by chance, in September when parliament was recalled, only one month after he had made those threats, we suddenly found that the tiger's roar had become the cat's purr.
Last week we saw more of the same. The hon. member for York South has been running around the countryside shouting threats of withdrawal of support, but when the crunch comes his party votes with the government. I find that hypocrisy rather repugnant. This is not the sort of behaviour which we ought to countenance. I am sure the NDP realizes that most Canadians find this kind of hypocrisy and this kind of behaviour intolerable. No doubt that is why the party is afraid to let go of the coat-tails of power and why it again stood behind its leader only a few days ago and voted with the government.
What about controls? We had a policy announcement last spring concerning the price freeze which was to be followed by a period of controls. The hon. member for York South, the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) and others nearly broke their necks running around the country telling people why they were against controls and why controls would not work. Now they are suddenly very much in favour of controls. They threatened to withdraw their support from the government unless it imposed controls.
The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands is a man whom we have grown to respect for his service to parliament and to the country. Even though I disagree with his ideas, he does what he thinks is right. Even he was unable to resist the temptation a couple of days ago to be a little devious when speaking on the energy situation. I asked the hon. member whether he was really in favour of controls. When we suggested them last February, he spoke against them. However, when he spoke a few days ago he was in favour of controls. His answer was, "Well, all you fellows are suggesting is a 90-day freeze." I do not

Energy Supplies Emergency Act believe he really meant that. If he did, it means he read only the first line of our policy paper and then ran around the country making statements based on that first line. If that was not the case, he was simply trying to be a little dishonest and I do not think he would want to do that.
This country is getting into a terrible mess as far as the economy, inflation and energy are concerned. It is not only the Liberals who are to blame; the New Democratic Party are also to blame because they are responsible for upholding this lame duck government. The NDP are maintaining this kind of a situation with a government that refuses to accept its responsibility and refuses to deal with major problems in an effective way. The NDP have to share the blame for this situation and they will have to account for their behaviour to the electorate when the time comes.
Before this bill is passed it would only be sensible for the standing committee to make a very exhaustive and extensive inquiry into all aspects of Canada's energy situation to determine the true extent of the crisis, if indeed there is a crisis. The committee should be empowered to call before it the minister, his advisers, representatives of the oil companies and anyone else knowledgeable about or concerned with the field of energy. Only after that kind of study would it be possible to decide whether there is a crisis and whether the minister really needs the kind of power he is seeking in this bill.
Before concluding I want to deal briefly with the question of the Athabasca tar sands. Syncrude, a consortium of companies, is prepared to construct an extraction plant with a capacity of 125,000 barrels a day. They are now prepared to go ahead. They have made an agreement with the province which will provide to the public treasury the maximum amount of revenue. If this project goes ahead it will mean more than 10,000 jobs in northern Alberta and in other parts of the country. It will mean that the town of Fort McMurray will more than double in population. It will be one of the initial steps in that region becoming a highly industrialized centre of Alberta and in due course a highly industrialized centre of Canada.
At the present time there are many huge construction projects of this kind in the making in North America. They require specialized materials and equipment, specially built metal receptacles and special tools and equipment of various kinds which are not mass produced. I am told that if these materials are ordered now, there is a waiting time of at least several months and possibly one to two years. The federal government should be a little more co-operative and a little more cognizant of the serious deleterious effects of holding up this project. The project is awaiting certain assurances from the federal government, or at least some clarification on where the federal government stands on the whole question. Until these matters are clarified the project will not proceed.
The minister should take a closer look at the significance of this project to Albertans and, indeed, to Canada as a whole, not just because we have a high unemployment situation and require the jobs that would be produced but because we have an energy shortage looming in the not too distant future. Plants such as that proposed by Syncrude cannot be built overnight; it is a matter of years before they are in production. I think we should proceed with this project as quickly as possible. I hope the minister will

take whatever action is necessary to get the project rolling without further delay.

Mr. Speaker, I note a good deal of impatience on the other side of the House and to my left. I hope they will bear with me as we examine this bill, look into each clause and see what it will mean to Canadians in all parts of the country. The hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner) really dug into what this energy problem or so-called crisis is all about. It is a transportation problem. We in Canada are self-sufficient in oil but we are not able to get it from one end of the country to the other.
I noted that some members of the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications asked the president of Canadian National Railways whether it would be possible to put liners in grain cars in order to move oil from Alberta and other parts of western Canada to the eastern market. That really points up the problem. At the present time the facilities are not available to move oil from Alberta, Saskatchewan and perhaps Manitoba to the eastern markets.
The hon. member for Crowfoot suggested that the port facilities to move oil through the Panama Canal to eastern Canada, or across Canada by pipeline or rail are inadequate at the present time. We should have anticipated this problem of eastern Canada being cut off from offshore oil, necessitating the transport of oil from western to eastern Canada by some method. I suspect that the best method to transport oil from one end of the country to the other is by pipeline. As some members have suggested, we should have looked into this pipeline four or five years ago, not now when we have shortages of all products and transportation problems. There is a shortage of the steel required to build a pipeline from Sarnia to Montreal, not to mention the looping that will be necessary on the Trans Canada pipeline to supply that oil.
Introducing the bill last week, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) stated it was analogous to an insurance policy. Shortly thereafter, my hon. friend from Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) asked him to disclose the specifics of that insurance policy, for example, what were the risks and how much was the premium. These questions have not been answered and I seriously doubt that they ever will be answered. I would be willing to bet that the minister's policy is of the short term, low dividend, variety. And maybe the minister, too, is of the short term, low dividend variety.
The bill before us is a glaring example of the kind of legislation we have so often been asked to consider. I have seen issues come and go, and generally the NDP find some way of making the issues go. Legislation is all too often hastily prepared and poorly researched. It is difficult to sort out all the contradictory statements we have heard in the past few weeks, not only from the minister of energy but from the Prime Minister. Only last week, for instance, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said he would like to see Canada become self-sufficient in energy by 1980. But

we are already exporting more oil than we are importing, so this country does not lack oil supplies for our own use.
There is, in fact, a great deal of capacity in Alberta as well as in other provinces which could quickly be reflected in terms of increased production.
