It is up to all of us, I guess. I realize there are many global and national issues with which we are confronted these days, but I do not think we should lose sight of what is essentially a problem that will continue to confront this government and successive governments in years to come unless we take the problem seriously. Perhaps I could put it best by simply saying that in the last few weeks I have had an opportunity, travelling in the Atlantic provinces and meeting with people both in government and in universities, to be made aware again of the real problems that exist. I intend to speak specifically about Atlantic Canada because that is the area I know best and, quite frankly, that is the area which conerns me most. The real problem that exists is in respect of the lack of accurate and relevant statistical information about the Atlantic provinces. Nothing could be more true to a member who comes from a constituency in the province of Prince Edward Island.
The latest indication of that came last week with the most recent set of statistics of employment, unemployment and changes in the cost of living. When a Prince Edward Islander looks at a report concerning employment, he is faced with very few numbers and a great many asterisks because he is told at the outset that most of the information which can be provided by the most knowledgeable statistical agency in the country, Statistics Canada, is not accurate. What we are told about November, 1973, in terms of employment is that in a general way the labour force represents some 40,000 people, and in a general way there are 36,000 people who were employed during that month. But with regard to unemployment and the unemployment rate no definitive answer can be given. The sort of simple answer for this, since I am not a statistician or an economist and cannot get into all the different quantum explanations, is that at the present time when computations are made in respect of employment and unemployment the figures are averaged to the nearest thousand.
The problem Statistics Canada has in reporting accurate figures for Prince Edward Island is that if there are 999 people unemployed in Prince Edward Island, it is suggested there are in fact less than 1,000 and therefore perhaps there is conceivably no one unemployed there. If the figure is raised to 1,001 by adding two more people to the unemployment rolls, suddenly the unemployment rate jumps in Prince Edward Island from zero to 2,000. That is the kind of confusion and misleading information you get, because Statistics Canada rightly refuses to report this kind of percentage as it would be ludicrous. Prince Edward Island is just one of the ten provinces of this country which receives this kind of information that represents just one of the serious shortcomings and anomalies in the present statistical information available from Statistics Canada.
In a few minutes I intend to mention some of the other problems in respect of our region in terms of having truly
December 14, 1973

adequate information in order to formulate economic and social policy. In spite of these difficulties we have the audacity-perhaps I should not say "we" because as members of parliament we do not really formulate government policy-but governments have the audacity day by day, week by week to enunciate programs to alleviate problems of unemployment and in respect of the cost of living based on this kind of misleading and, if I can use the term, half-baked information. This happens in a day and age when we know we have gone far beyond the times of Francis Bacon who said many years ago that knowledge is power. We might say today, perhaps paraphrasing some of the information that comes to us from such works as "Future Shock" by Toffler, that knowledge is a key component to change and accelerating knowledge acquisition means accelerating change.
We must have accurate information if government programs which involve billions of dollars of public money are to do the job they are meant to do. To repeat what I said a little earlier, as I visited people who are concerned with human development and social improvement in the Atlantic provinces, people who analyse this question in a detached way in university communities and people who try to work with relevant information in government offices, I found that they cannot do so and they ask, "Why can't we have accurate information and statistics about our provinces, about parts of our provinces and about the region as a whole?" I have introduced this very modest bill-members who have looked at it will see it is very modest-to make the point again that unless Statistics Canada, in gathering the information it gathers day by day, can really do the job it is meant to do, then in terms of formulating social and economic policy we are wasting a great deal of money which could be much better spent.
Many of us who live in the Atlantic provinces think we know what the situation is in regard to our own province and our own region, but we know in real terms that often we can be very much shocked when we see the actual statistics. Just yesterday I had the opportunity of meeting some representatives of the bilingual districts commission who have done a rather intensive study of the language changes occurring within my constituency of Egmont. They were frank to admit that one of the difficulties they had was that they really had to base their conclusions on a rather rough compilation of statistics taken once every ten years-1961, 1971, and so on-and that to try to formulate sensible recommendations in respect of the bilingual complexion for the future of the Egmont constituency would require a great deal more relevant information that is presently available.
Some members may recall that only a few years ago, in early 1971, for the first time in the Atlantic region the Atlantic Development Council produced a strategy. I do not intend to get into the merits or otherwise of that strategy produced by the ministerial advisory council for the Atlantic region. One of the very clear recommendations that they put on the record at that time was as follows, and I read from page 13, recommendation 65:
Data relevant to the economy of the Atlantic provinces are with reference to some subjects, and in some respects, seriously inadequate to provide a basis for the formulation of policies and pro-
Statistics Act
grams and their subsequent monitoring. The Council has found this a serious problem which has hampered and complicated the preparation of a development strategy. Now that a comprehensive development effort has been launched, steps must be taken to correct this situation.
The council may have been somewhat overoptimistic about a comprehensive development strategy, but to the degree that such a strategy has not been inaugurated it may well be attributable to the fact that we do not have adequate statistics for the Atlantic region. We are faced with a variety of problems in this regard. Much of the statistical information for the Local Initiatives Program, which we were told in the beginning was to be allocated on the basis of unemployment and other social indicators across the country, we find-and I will not get into some of the allegations of political bias-to be based on the 1971 census.
We know only too well that in the period since 1971 a great deal has happened both in terms of the mobility of people and in terms of the economic situation in this country. As recently as this week we learned that across the country, especially in the larger urban centres in the central part of the country, unemployment has been on the decrease, but in the Atlantic provinces unemployment has increased in some places. In some parts of the Atlantic provinces it has increased dramatically, so dramatically that it is difficult to explain.
I have attempted to analyse-again with inadequate figures-the fact that in some of the urban centres in the Atlantic provinces, such as Halifax, Saint John and Fredericton, until two months ago unemployment was down 3 per cent or 4 per cent, and there has been a rather unusual job vacancy situation in some of the larger urban centres. But Statistics Canada is reporting as late as this week that we have a 9.6 per cent unemployment rate in the Atlantic provinces, a 13.6 per cent rate in Newfoundland and 9.9 per cent in New Brunswick. When I try to investigate the situation in Nova Scotia alone, because I thought that being the largest province in population I would find reasonable statistical explanations, I find that Cape Breton has an unemployment rate of 12 per cent and Nova Scotia about 8 per cent, but no one seems to know the explanation for this in terms of regional inconsistencies.
What we are trying to do, quite obviously, is to solve modern social and economic problems with horse and buggy statistics. The time has come to go beyond the horse and buggy stage, to realize that the nature of government and the intervention of government, not only federal government but other levels of government as well, has changed so dramatically in the past decade that to rely on normal social indicators is to waste the time of the general public and to destroy the effectiveness of programs that attempt to focus on the real human problems that exist.
Another example of the situation in the Atlantic provinces is the fact that for years-I do not know how long this goes back but I have statistics, unreliable as they may be, showing that at least for the last two decades-there has been a tremendous amount of out-migration from the Atlantic region. We know that as late as the mid 1960s there was a net out-migration of as many as 25,000 or 35,000 who had left the Atlantic region for other parts of this country or perhaps the United States.

December 14, 1973
Statistics Act
Then we are told that in 1972 there has been a net in-migration for the first time in, I do not know how long. One would have to go back 30 or 40 years. The in-migration in 1972 amounted to some 5,000 people. We do not have enough information, unfortunately, to tell us in what way or in what form these people arrived and who they are, nor where they have gone and why they have come into the region. We do not have the gross figures on migration in or out, and we are left with the situation of trying to formulate economic and social policy without understanding what these semi-statistics tell us.
I want to quote for a moment from a speech that was given by a lady who has some interest in the subject on which I am speaking today. Her name is Sylvia Ostry. Some years ago, Dr. Ostry made a speech in which she made a few interesting comments which I think it might be worth relaying to the members of this House. She suggests in this speech, which I found to be an excellent talk about new directions, that we have to find some new social indicators because the nature of government planning and government action has changed so dramatically.
She suggested that we must develop-
-an emphasis on anticipatory rather than reactive decision making: an emphasis on systems rather than on discrete problem or policy areas. If one stresses the need to anticipate rather than react to problems and recognizes that inter relationships among proposed solutions must be explicitly taken into account, this*may lead to a more careful and meaningful exploration of social priorities and effective strategies for their ultimate attainment.
Later in her speech she spoke about the need for-
-an increasingly articulated need by individuals within contemporary affluent societies to exercise more real choice about how they will live.
In the final part of her speech she suggested the following:
-the movement to develop what have been called "social indicators", direct measures of social welfare or distress such as indexes of mental and physical health; social mobility; public order and safety; the quality of the environment; participation and alienation, etc.
She went on to suggest that without these kinds of new statistics we will not be able to do the job adequately in terms of meeting and responding to the changes that are taking place in our society. I suppose that the best example of the situation in which we find ourselves today is the energy crisis. Here we are in a very difficult situation because we have not even begun to think of how we would quantify, how we would gather and how we would display the kind of information on energy utilization, energy needs and energy development either for the whole of the country or for the part of the country which is in most serious jeopardy at present either due to the potential petroleum shortages or to the very rapid rise in prices that has occurred. It points up, again, the lack of foresight that we have had and perhaps the lack of encouragement that we have given to our key statistical and information gathering system, that is, Statistics Canada.
Why do I spend so much time talking about the need for better information? It comes down very simply to this: I think at no time has it been clearer than in the last few months under this government that a good social and economic policy cannot be formulated flying by the seat of one's pants, and it certainly cannot happen because some-

body gets up on a specific morning and decides he will have such and such a program or such and such a policy. We have had far too many months and far too many programs of "ad hockery." If we are to get beyond that, if we are to get positive and active government we will not get it unless we establish adequate benchmarks for social and economic development. We cannot begin to establish either short-term or long-term goals unless we have the information, the measurements and the monitoring to make them a practical reality. That is why I hope hon. members this afternoon will support the speedy passage and recommendation of this bill to committee.

subtopic: STATISTICS ACT
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AUTHORIZE COLLECTION OF ECONOMIC AND SOCIAL STATISTICS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was pleased that the hon. member for Egmont (Mr. MacDonald) proposed his amendment and recognized that there was a small error in the drafting. I agree with him that it is insignificant and that the question we are really debating this afternoon is the substance of the bill. I listened very carefully to the hon. member, and I was pleased to hear his comment that he was looking for better information and not necessarily for more information. I am not convinced that we need more surveys, polls and inquiries. It may be that fewer would be in order.
I wonder whether the hon. member, before preparing the amendment, considered who does the work in most of these surveys. I suggest that a good portion of it has to be done by the small businessmen in Canada and, for that matter, by the larger corporations; but they hire staff and write off the cost as a business expense. The small businessman finds himself inundated with inquiries. Since Statistics Canada has been in operation for a number of years, it seems to me that the time has come to establish some form of task force to look into the kind of information that both Statistics Canada and provincial governments are gathering.
Just the other day a small businessman in my riding sent me a folder that contained seven or eight pages of questions. It had his name at the top and his address. It asked for all kinds of information, what kind of work he engaged in, how many employers he had, what he was paying them and what deductions were taken off at source. I got tired reading the questions because the list was so long. On the surface there did not seem to be an adequate explanation of the reason for it. Ture, Statistics Canada talks about such information being confidential, but the small businessman has a right to be a little apprehensive and to wonder how many people actually are looking at the type of information that he has to provide in this way.
The crowning blow for this individual was that he was told he had to complete the questionnaire and that if he did not complete it then under the act he would be subject to a fine. I can appreciate that one of the costs of doing business in Canada calls for completing income tax forms, preparing T-4 slips for employees and even collecting sales tax for the provinces and remitting it to the provincial treasury, but it seems to me we add insult to injury for the small businessman when we send him a leaflet full of questions which he cannot throw in the waste-paper basket. If it were a voluntary matter he could make up his own mind about filling out the questionnaire or throwing
December 14, 1973

it in a waste-paper basket. But the government agencies seeking the information have the sanction of legislation behind them and as a result the small businessman is not told that he may, at his choice, fill out the questionnaire or not fill it out; he is told he must fill it out.
Like the hon. member, I sometimes wonder if some people come into their offices in the morning, sit down and ask each other whether they should hold a survey on a particular subject, seeking information to help the small businessman to expand, telling him what kind of equipment would be better to use in his particular business. But I wonder if they would be a little more careful in sending out questionnaires to businessmen if they had to pay each businessman $10 for the time he had to devote to completing questionnaires. I wonder if that would limit the number of questionnaires that do go out, and if more careful thought would be given to the kinds of questions asked and to the length of the questionnaires. I have mentioned a figure of $10, but I suggest that the small businessman's time is worth very much more than that simply because of the length of time he has to devote to giving information to the federal, provincial and municipal governments.
I agree that the time has come for an investigation to be made by a task force or some other appropriate authority into the kind of information gathering that is done in Canada, to determine if it is really necessary to have all of these papers that come over the desk of the small businessman. In spite of my comments, Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to be negative about Statistics Canada. I know that many of the surveys it conducts are necessary. But the businessman, when he fills out these forms, is probably asking himself - of course, in the first place he is angry because he has to do it - who is going to benefit? He has spent 15 years building up this information, learning through trial and error that this particular way is the best in which to operate his business; he wonders if all this information is going to be culled from him to be used by somebody else who has not had to go through the school of hard knocks, who can take advantage of this information and perhaps become established in competition with him. By reading the answers he gives, somebody else may prosper.
Further, Mr. Speaker, the time has come for such a study to be made in order to avoid duplication. As a man who practised law for some 10 or 12 years, although I had a modest business engaging only a few employees I know the amount of paperwork that came over my desk and had to be attended to on behalf of government. I agree that part of it is proper. It is the expense of doing business in Canada, and here I speak of Ontario, the area with which I am most familiar. But on more than one occasion I saw the same questions being asked by the municipal government, the provincial government and the federal government. I was asked why I selected that particular site for my business. The municipality wanted to know for planning purposes but I do not know why the provincial government and the federal government wanted the same information.
I wish to enter a plea with Statistics Canada and other governmental information gathering agencies that they take a long, hard look at the surveys they are conducting
Statistics Act
and at the results they publish. I sometimes wonder if they really are significant without having all the background and explanations provided. Here I am thinking of things such as the monthly unemployment figures. They come out with the seasonally adjusted figure and the number of people actually unemployed at a particular time. Yet the survey done, I think, is incomplete because of the actual number of people contacted. It is said that for statistical purposes 1,000 people contacted will be as accurate as one million contacted. Frankly, Mr. Speaker, I do not think the people connected with Statistics Canada ever ran in an election, where you can find that after the first thousand votes come in you might be ten behind, but when the next 20,000 votes come in and are counted you end up with a tremendous victory. I think they miss things like that.
This subject is something in which I have been interested ever since I was first elected to this House in 1968. At that time I had many calls from small businessmen in my area. We were examining the question of setting up secondary industry in Sarnia where there is already heavy industry and there is competition between industry with respect to wages. One of the things we discovered with respect to doing business in an area like Sarnia is the fact that all these additional forms, figures ans surveys add to the cost of doing business. Those concerned suggested that if even part of that cost could be eliminated it would be a tremendous help.
As a government supporter and as a member of parliament, I realized there are two sides to the question. I tried to explain to the businessmen that many of the surveys which are done are done with good motives, with the idea of aiding and assisting them. But I have determined from my research that some of the Statistics Canada business surveys are undertaken merely for the purpose of keeping administrative records. Each of these sources in general provides both national, and, to a varying extent, regional data. The hon. member indicates that they do not go into small enough regions as far as he is concerned. I think there is provision in section 3(e) to go into regional areas, but I think there has to be some form of motivation, either that the minister of industry for the province or the treasury has indicated that it would help them to determine where to locate industry, for example, in Prince Edward Island if they had more specific information on an area the size of the hon. member's riding let alone the size of Prince Edward Island.
I think that is good and that kind of information would be very helpful. I sometimes wonder if it would not be much more helpful than the countless hours that are spent on broad surveys that are very interesting to read in the newspaper, but when you throw the paper out, out goes the information on the survey. I think if we got down to a little more focusing on the kinds of information that the hon. member is looking for, maybe there would be a better role to be played by government departments. One of the defences put up by the department is that in these business surveys location is a meaningful concept. This comes back to the question, "Why did you locate in your particular area?" In my law office days I located in my particular area because it was the only upstairs office I could find

December 14, 1973
Statistics Act
that I could afford. I gave the same answer to all the questionnaires, but they indicated that in the business surveys where location is a meaningful concept, like manufacturing and mining, the data are tabulated regionally and the releases are only subject to the confidentiality provisions of the Statistics Act. I assume, Mr. Speaker, that means they remove the name of the corporation which provided the information, and to that extent it is confidential when it is sent out.
In other business surveys where location is not a meaningful concept, for example, transportation and communication, they indicate regional tabulations cannot be carried out. In the case of household sample surveys, here I suppose if someone is at home they may not feel quite so strongly about these forms that have to be filled out, although I know that the busy housewife nowadays feels she has better things to do than to answer surveys. Certainly we find that with Air Canada passengers: when they are handed a slip at the airport I suspect that often it goes into the waste basket at the end of the long corridor. But in the case of household sample surveys, the extent to which regional data can be provided is limited by sample size. As sample size decreases, so does the amount of statistically reliable regional detail which is available. That is my point exactly.
Rather than concentrating on a wide area, I think it would be more appropriate if they focused on a small area and did a more significant and meaningful study. If you do a large area and a few people, the department itself tells you that as the size decreases so does the reliability of the statistics. I suggest, with respect, if you have that on a small scale, on going over a larger area you are really cutting down the statistical reliability but over a wider area. It seems to me that is hardly progress. The high cost of survey-taking makes it important for the bureau to consider carefully the sample size, that is, the cost. I think if we added one more cost factor, tha is, paying businessmen for filling out some of these forms, maybe we would have fewer surveys and they would be focused in smaller areas.
Mr. Speaker, I understand there are other members who wish to speak. I think I have made the point that I wanted to make and on that basis I will resume my seat.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall detain the House for only a few minutes. May I say at the outset that if hon. members were not unanimously prepared to discuss Bill C-10 this afternoon, this is a good one for us to be dealing with, and I commend the hon. member for Egmont (Mr. MacDonald) for presenting this bill. As I understand it, his desire is that the quality of our statistics be improved and his bill suggests that one of the ways in which to do that is to provide, in certain instances, for statistics to be obtained on an area basis.
I know that when he uses the word "area" he has in mind geographical areas, but I should like to suggest that there is also room for statistics being gathered on the basis of social areas. In particular I am thinking about the consumer price index, popularly known as the cost of living index, which is produced by Statistics Canada. If I understand it correctly, this is one index right across the whole spectrum of society. However, there are certain

groups, old age pensioners, veterans and, commencing in 1974, recipients of family allowances to whom the consumer price index is not just a statistic but is the basis on which the amount of money they will receive is determined.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the cost of living increase experienced by the whole community might not be close at all to the actual impact of a cost of living increase on old age pensioners, veterans or mothers with children for whom they are receiving family allowances. When you are an old age pensioner, the kinds of things that you may have to buy are of a limited number and, as I say, that cost of living factor can be quite different from the factor for the entire community.
I would hope that when the people at Statistics Canada look at this debate and consider whether ways may be found to improve the quality of our statistics, they will consider the desirability of statistics that show what is the actual cost of living increase for groups like old age pensioners, veterans and mothers in receipt of family allowances. People who are in receipt of these benefits are forever surprised when they get their increases because in their experience the cost of living has gone up for them much more than is reflected in their pension increases. I think this problem could be met if we had statistics computed on the basis of social areas as well as on the basis of geographic areas.
I have one other sentence and then I shall sit down, Mr. Speaker. I liked the reference by the hon. member for Egmont, or maybe it was a quotation from Dr. Sylvia Ostry before she became Chief Statistician, that maybe it is time for us to be making anticipatory rather than reactive decisions. I think this is true particularly in the area of enabling people, especially pensioners and others, to cope with the rising cost of living.

speakeroldname: Mr. Pierre De Bane (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: STATISTICS ACT

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in substance the amendment introduced by the hon. member for Egmont (Mr. MacDonald) is appropriate and deserves the support of all hon. members.
I say in substance because I think there has been too great a tendency in this country to consider only national statistics, national aggregates, and not often enough the statistics of various areas which differ substantially from national statistics.
Having said that I have doubts about the advisability of the hon. member's amendment which would not produce the results he seeks because it would frustrate the clause he wants to replace and which seems to me to be very important and very useful.
As to regionalizing our statistics I think more should be done in that respect. Our bureau of statistics, now called Statistics Canada, is certainly one of the most competent in the world. Very few countries have available to them a statistical department so up to date, so specialized, so competent, so careful and impartial such as Statistics Canada, which is headed so competently by Mrs. Sylvia Ostry.
Furthermore, I think Statistics Canada should try and do more. I understand that such an undertaking is pre-
December 14, 1973

vented from taking place mainly because of a lack of funds. If Statistics Canada had more money it could compile a lot more statistics in many more areas. Nevertheless, new studies have to be made. I am sure that all hon. members would be interested in seeing Statistics Canada undertake studies on various questions of interest to the people of this country.
To mention only one, I have been personally interested for some time in the distribution of doctors in Canada and I am trying to obtain data on this subject. Unfortunately, I have not been able to secure any figures from anyone to show exactly which region is short of doctors and how many specialists are lacking in certain regions.
The contribution of the hon. member for Egmont who reminded us how greatly differ regional statistics from national statistics, was quite eloquent about the LIP program. For instance, we know that this year the budget for this program was substantially reduced under the pretense that national unemployment was down by 1 per cent.
I would quote a few figures supplied by the Canada Manpower Centre in my constituency of Matane. In Matane, out of 3,360 people on the labour market, 1,344 are unemployed namely 40 per cent and this in the chief town of my constituency. If you consider now the villages surrounding this town whether it be Petite-Matane, St-Andelme, Sainte-Felicite, Grosses-Roches, Les Capucins, you find that the unemployment rate varies from 65 to 70 per cent. In other places such as Sainte-Paule, Les Boules, Metis, it is as high as 75 per cent.
Imagine what the reaction would be throughout the country if the unemployment rate were to reach 10 or 15 per cent at the national level. It would be a terrible crisis. The public coffers would be wide open and we would accumulate huge deficits to stimulate the economy while such sad situations as those I just mentioned would be of very small importance at the national policy level. And yet those situations have been existing for decades. Those regions are so under-populated that the fact that those people are working or not hardly puts a dent in national statistics.
For instance, in the Gaspe area about 60,000 people are on the labour market out of which about 30,000 are idle. Even if they were working they would not affect the national statistics but I can assure the House that as regards social peace and the economic welfare of this region, statistics such as those affect people's morale, which is absolutely unacceptable.
That is why, Mr. Speaker, I wish to say in concluding how much I approve the proposal from the hon. member for Egmont to regionalize statistics a little more and make them more available. That is a somewhat different question, but it is really related to the first one and the way the hon. member went about it unfortunately does not seem to me the most appropriate way of proceeding.
That being said, I wish again to give credit to the group of public servants, under the extremely able direction of Mrs. Ostry, for their efficiency and fair mindedness, and I hope Parliament will earmark greater funds for that agency so as to enable it to make more intensive inquiries. I mentioned the one about statistics related to the regional
Statistics Act
unemployment rate, the allocation of doctors and the statistics on poverty in our area. So many other fields would deserve an inquiry on the part of Statistics Canada, something which is not to being done because of a restricted budget.
Mr. Speaker, I believe there is a consensus in the House so that the work already done for the regionalization of statistics be carried on, for this country, as was often said, has several areas which are very different from one another and it would be our biggest error if we were to apply limited and standard measures in a country as big and as diversified as ours.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I certainly appreciate the point being made. However, I thought it was not a bad idea to make some general observations in my opening remarks about things which pertain to the general area from which the author of this proposal and I come. It is in that context that I wish to make a few remarks. I see the

December 14, 1973
Statistics Act
clock is moving on and I am afraid there will not be time for me to make all the points I wished to make. In any case, after listening to the hon. member for Egm'ont I feel that the suggested amendment is redundant. What he seeks through his amendment has already been well taken care of in the Statistics Act which was amended, I think, in 1971.
I have been assured that there is a special research staff with special responsibility for developing estimates of socioeconomic data for some provincial areas, as well as a provincial liaison and consultative services staff which has prime responsibility for working with provincial government departments and groups of regional provincial governments such as we have in the Atlantic area. For example, this can be useful in the context of the proposed cooperative union of the Maritime provinces. These services are co-ordinated for general or specific assistance in the statistical field.
It seems that some provinces are a little timid or hesitant at times to request services that are available. Most times it is just a matter of getting on the phone or dropping a note to the Chief Statistician on behalf of any provincial government and requesting chat special studies be made. It is in that sense the amendment is redundant. I have also been assured that for many years Statistics Canada has worked very closely through conferences and meetings with provincial government departments to develop meaningful statistics at both the provincial and subprovincial levels. That is the main point I wish to make today. I hope there will be an opportunity later to go into this proposition a little more deeply. I hope to be back here in future sessions, and I do not see any problem next year.
I agree with the substance of the bill. Perhaps we can enjoin Statistics Canada to continue this excellent work and branch out into more specific areas of information gathering that are not available unless specific requests are made for them. I think a lot of this information could be made public without waiting for someone to come by, knock on the door and ask for it.

speakeroldname: Mr. Herb Breau (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subtopic: STATISTICS ACT
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AUTHORIZE COLLECTION OF ECONOMIC AND SOCIAL STATISTICS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall take just a few minutes because I believe it is my duty to point out a few things on the technical side. I agree in substance with what the hon. member proposes. If I had more time, I would expound on a lot of things he said and support them. In this bill the hon. member seeks to amend the act of 1948. That act was replaced with a new act in 1971 called the Statistics Act. The relevant section is 3(e). I suggest this section is even better than the one suggested by the hon. member because of one line at the end. The hon. member's amendment reads:
(d) generally to organize a scheme of co-ordinated social and
economic statistics pertaining to the whole of Canada, to each of the provinces thereof-
Up to that point it is the same as the old act. The hon. member has added:
-and to any area of Canada the minister may from time to time designate.
I would point out to the hon. member that the last part of section 3(e) reads:
-and to coordinate plans for the integration of such statistics.
I submit that these words are important. I believe the hon. member agrees. There is a lot of power in the Statistics Act to deal with this, and I do not think the hon. member would want to delete the words at the end of section 3(e). I just want to point this out to explain why we believe we should not proceed with this bill as it now stands. I want to make it abundantly clear that I believe the substance of it is important. I believe we should get better information in certain regions of the country. However, I am very concerned about definitions or impressions that form a part of the statistics that are taken across the country. They do not take into consideration the way of life of the different components of the economy. For example, they do not take into consideration the economic way of life in the Maritimes. More often than not the consumer price index and unemployment statistics do not define in economic terms the status of the economy. As the hon. member stated, they are not a good economic indicator.
In many places in my constituency and other parts of the Atlantic provinces it is impossible to work in the winter or during a certain time of the year. For example, employees in the logging industry and the pulp industry live in rural areas. The roads are not of the same standard as in other areas. Companies do not keep their camps open year-round, so it is not possible for the people to work year-round. These types of situations in certain areas are of importance.
Not only do we require better information, but in the future we should try to define the economic indicators and the socioeconomic indicators in those areas. That is where we should start. Despite the weakness of the bill from a legal standpoint, in substance it is very good and I commend the hon. member for bringing it before the House.
